subsubtopic: PROPOSED REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under Standing Order 43. Because capital punishment is such an emotional issue that quite obviously the government is unable to cope with it and because of the fact that this same government does not even uphold its own laws in respect of capital punishment, and because of the hesitancy to adhere to the wishes of what is now obviously the majority of Canadians who are in fact being asked to accept the alarming growth of crime as a way of life, and on the basis that this is indeed an urgent and pressing matter which deals with life and death, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurlburt):
That this parliament instruct the Prime Minister to initiate a national referendum with regard to capital punishment.

subsubtopic: FACILITIES BY MANAGEMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to propose a motion under Standing Order 43 arising from a number of instances, including Tuesday's manipulation and misuse by the CBC president, Mr. Picard, of publicly owned news facilities on the "World at Six" and the national television news to slander a member of this House, and last night's reprehensible prevention by CBC management of the same programs carrying the rebuttal given Picard's actions in the House yesterday, constituting management rather than editing of news, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That the House requests the Canadian Radio-Television Commission to hold a public inquiry into the existence of disgraceful manipulation and misuse of publicly owned CBC news facilities by CBC management, particularly by President Laurent Picard, for personal and political purposes that are not consistent with the principle of unbiased coverage of the news and that such inquiry also specifically determine whether or not such actions are encouraged, requested, or in any way arranged by persons in the Government of Canada.

speechtext:

WHEAT-SUGGESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF METHODS TO PREVENT LOSSES TO PRODUCERS AS RESULT OF LABOUR-MANAGEMENT DISPUTES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In the light of reliable statements released by the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association that the wheat producers of Canada have incurred losses of $261 million during the 1974-75 crop year as a result of labour disruptions and breakdowns in the grain handling and transportation system, which is the equivalent of 50 cents per bushel or $1,700 per producer, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart):
That the subject matter be referred to a special parliamentary committee to immediately consider ways and means of resolving the current labour-management relationship-to consider ways and means by which the producers may recover: and be further saved from any future losses as a result of the failure of management and/or labour to act responsibly in the over-all national interest.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S ESTIMATE OF NUMBER OF STARTS THIS YEAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. subtopic: DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF WARRANTY PROGRAM
DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF WARRANTY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a question for the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. In view of the fact the hon. Minister's predecessor in 1974 was promising a housing warranty program so that housing quality would be assured in Canada, and since almost a year later, on February 28, 1975, the minister responsible was still promising that concrete measures would be taken to implement a warranty program, is the minister now ready to inform the House if this program has either fallen
June 19, 1975

through or if it is to be implemented in the immediate future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF WARRANTY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows we are in consultation with the provinces, with the builders and consumers and everyone involved in this independent warranty plan on a national basis. In so far as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is concerned, we could implement one and would be quite prepared to do it in a very short period of time with relation to our programs. What we would like to see is a national program applied to all home building across the country. The provinces are co-operating fully as is the industry, the consumers and suppliers. We are giving it a very high priority. Meetings are taking place on a regular basis at which the provinces are present. I have every expectation of meeting the goal of later this year which I indicated in the House the other day.

subtopic: DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION OF WARRANTY PROGRAM
speechtext: A supplementary question. In view of the fact that some of the provinces are now going ahead with their own home warranty program is this indicative of the minister's ability to achieve consensus and agreement on this pressing issue in Canada's housing policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
maintopic: MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE SHORTAGE OF RENTAL ACCOMMODATION-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN ALLOCATION OF MONEY TO AHOP AND LIMITED DIVIDEND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have always said that we give a very high priority to rental accommodation. The most recent step has been the $200 million for limited dividend rental accommodation and we continue to give it that priority.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES-MEETING WITH SASKATCHEWAN FEDERATION OF INDIANS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SECOND QUARTER FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Under what pretence did he meet with 120 native people from the Saskatchewan Federation of Indians yesterday who came here to voice their specific concerns but who were forced to hear the minister delivering a 40-minute speech, until he was interrupted. Is that the kind of communication which took place in connection with the guidelines? Is that how consultation was carried on?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES-MEETING WITH SASKATCHEWAN FEDERATION OF INDIANS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SECOND QUARTER FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member's arithmetic is wrong. The speech was considerably shorter. However, that is not germane. What is germane is that we held discussions and, finally, I think the message got through to the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians, as it had to the Alberta Indian Association, the Union of New Brunswick Indians and the Union of Nova Scotia Indians long ago, to this effect: that if they will only sit down and discuss these problems and say where they think specific difficulties with the guidelines lie, we would be prepared to change and amend them. I think the onus is on them. They have come forward with no specific proposals, no precise suggestions. They have indicated now that they want to meet with me and come forward with their precise suggestions, which is what the other groups have been doing for months.

subtopic: LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES-MEETING WITH SASKATCHEWAN FEDERATION OF INDIANS-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SECOND QUARTER FUNDING

June 19, 1975

that their second quarter funding will be granted even though they may not have had time to enter appeals, since the July deadline will soon be here.

maintopic: JAMES SMITH RESERVE-ALLEGATION NATIVES REFUSED SUPPORT FOR THEIR CHILDREN UNLESS LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES SIGNED

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
maintopic: JAMES SMITH RESERVE-ALLEGATION NATIVES REFUSED SUPPORT FOR THEIR CHILDREN UNLESS LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES SIGNED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following on the question which has just been asked, may I remind the minister of the reply he gave me on June 4, as reported on page 6429 of Hansard, when he said that the Indians were not being coerced or forced in any way. I immediately challenged that statement, because in the province of Saskatchewan and on the particular Indian reserve to which I referred then, the James Smith reserve, the Indians have been refused support for their children unless they sign these guidelines and accept them. That does not look very much like the kind of co-operation which should be expected between the government, untied by bureaucratic autocracy, and the representatives of the Indians.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: JAMES SMITH RESERVE-ALLEGATION NATIVES REFUSED SUPPORT FOR THEIR CHILDREN UNLESS LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES SIGNED
speechtext: Order, please. Surely, the right hon. member realizes that he is entering into debate instead of asking a question. If the right hon. member has a question to ask, perhaps he will ask it.

maintopic: JAMES SMITH RESERVE-ALLEGATION NATIVES REFUSED SUPPORT FOR THEIR CHILDREN UNLESS LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES SIGNED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find it impossible to impinge on the mentality of the Indian department with an ordinary question. I ask this: Considering what has happened on this particular Indian reserve and on others, where people are being forced to accept guidelines they don't want, will the minister do something at once to bring about support for the children, the boys and girls on these reserves, so that they will have the necessary food; for starvation faces them because they dared to stand for a principle.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: JAMES SMITH RESERVE-ALLEGATION NATIVES REFUSED SUPPORT FOR THEIR CHILDREN UNLESS LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES SIGNED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with respect, that simply is not fact. All I have to say is that Chief Ahena-kew, the president of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians, and the right hon. member's good friend, the vice president, Solomon Sanderson, indicated that they would like to meet with me before July 1 and finally come forward with some concrete suggestions for the guidelines. I indicated that I would be happy to meet them.

maintopic: JAMES SMITH RESERVE-ALLEGATION NATIVES REFUSED SUPPORT FOR THEIR CHILDREN UNLESS LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES SIGNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs, the Indian Association of Alberta and the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians are opposed to these guidelines. Why should they, the first people of our country, be intimidated in this way when they are actually wards of the Queen and so regard themselves to be? Will the minister endeavour to break himself loose 
from the enthralment of bureaucratic tyranny being practiced against the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: JAMES SMITH RESERVE-ALLEGATION NATIVES REFUSED SUPPORT FOR THEIR CHILDREN UNLESS LOCAL GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES SIGNED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as far as the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs is concerned, they are off on a different tack right now. I have had no representations or expressions from British Columbia concerning the guidelines. As you know, they indicated they wish to reject federal government funding totally. In the province of Alberta, as I indicated, I spoke a couple of days ago to the president of the Alberta Indian Association. He gave me a reply directly contrary to what the right hon. member just said. I have already indicated what is going on in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF INDUSTRIES ON THE SOUTH SHORE OF THE ST. LAWRENCE TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF INDUSTRIES ON THE SOUTH SHORE OF THE ST. LAWRENCE TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
Since the province of Quebec has a very important area which is known generally as the south shore region, part of which includes the Bellechasse riding, and since there are a great many unemployed in this area, can the minister advise the House whether he has had consultations with the Quebec government about a possible program to attract new industries or expand existing ones in the area, in order to create jobs and find use for the qualified workers who are available there at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF INDUSTRIES ON THE SOUTH SHORE OF THE ST. LAWRENCE TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, personally, in a general way, I have discussed the region of Quebec to which the hon. member refers along with a number of others where developmental opportunities are important. As well, I know that my officials, including those who are resident in the province of Quebec and in Quebec City, have also been discussing these matters with the provincial government. I do not immediately know the current stage of those discussions. I will be pleased to make inquiries and get an up-to-date report for the hon. member.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF INDUSTRIES ON THE SOUTH SHORE OF THE ST. LAWRENCE TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a supplementary. Without wanting to give to understand that the federal and Quebec governments showed greater interest in the Montreal and Quebec City regions, I should like to insist on asking him whether he is willing, as the person in charge of regional economic expansion, to make representations, if necessary, to the government of the province of Quebec for the establishment of a very specific program in the south shore region so that for once the population of that region will not feel neglected and may in its turn receive benefits and aid enabling it to expand and use the manpower available in the region?
June 19, 1975

subtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF INDUSTRIES ON THE SOUTH SHORE OF THE ST. LAWRENCE TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. I simply point out to the hon. member that many regions of Quebec, other than the Montreal and Quebec city areas which he mentioned, have received attention. Indeed, only a couple of months ago a number of areas strategically located throughout the province were designated for the creation of, for example, industrial parks. I will be glad to discuss with the hon. member the specific geographic region he has in mind and to initiate specific talks along those lines with the government of Quebec, if it has not been done already, but I suspect it has.

maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR DELAY IN ACTION BY FEDERAL DEPARTMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR DELAY IN ACTION BY FEDERAL DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare, one of whose inspectors yesterday testified before the crime commission in Montreal that the federal government knew about the meat situation in the Province of Quebec as far back as 1968 and that by January, 1974, the situation was, to quote him, so serious as to be frightening. I should like to ask the minister why this situation was allowed to continue for so long, indeed, to continue until the crime commission was appointed in Quebec, and why, in the words of the inspector, no tangible results were achieved from any of the efforts made by the hon. gentleman's department? Yet this public inquiry appointed by the government of Quebec immediately gets results.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR DELAY IN ACTION BY FEDERAL DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be pleased to send to the Leader of the Opposition a copy of the testimony of the inspector in which he will find an answer to his questions. He will even note that the inspector has clearly shown before the committee that the necessary inquiry could only be carried out by the police force with its facilities available for that purpose. It was impossible with the indications which my inspectors had to provide any evidence.

maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR DELAY IN ACTION BY FEDERAL DEPARTMENT
speechtext: In view of the evidence of the inspector that he was not able to get any results in 1973 and that the police, when they were called in, were not getting any results either, why did the minister not take some other course of action such as the appointment of a public inquiry? As we know, a public inquiry did get results eventually. Is there any way in which the minister can justify this situation being allowed to continue from 1968 to 1975?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR DELAY IN ACTION BY FEDERAL DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can merely speak about the period during which I was minister, but I can give the assurance to the Leader of the Opposition that the inquiry
Oral Questions
carried out by the police force gave some results. They have been submitted to the commission which would have been unable to discover what it did find out without the work performed by the police force throughout the inquiry.

maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ACT UNDER FOOD AND DRUGS ACT

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ACT UNDER FOOD AND DRUGS ACT
speechtext:
Was the
government of Canada aware that meat unfit for human consumption was being sold in the Province of Quebec as far back as 1968, as appears from the sworn testimony given in Montreal by an inspector from the hon. gentleman's department? If so, can the minister explain why he did not proceed under the Food and Drugs Act regardless of any inquiry which was taking place in Quebec, especially since the present inquiry has nothing to do directly with the meat situation? The current revelations are merely incidental to an inquiry into organized crime in Quebec.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ACT UNDER FOOD AND DRUGS ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat once again that suspicions existed as far back as 1968. As the inspector concerned indicated very clearly, there were consultations with police authorities to determine whether it was possible to obtain any subsequent evidence. It seems that that could not then be done. As I pointed out in the House previously, new efforts were made later on, they were successful, as evidenced by the inquiry now going on in Quebec. Once more, I shall be happy to give the hon. member a copy of the testimony of the inspector concerned, which shows very well the efforts made by my department during that whole period.

maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-INQUIRY WHETHER FEDERAL DEPARTMENT INFORMED QUEBEC OR ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA OF SITUATION

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's West):
maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-INQUIRY WHETHER FEDERAL DEPARTMENT INFORMED QUEBEC OR ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA OF SITUATION
speechtext: I apologize if this further question sounds repetitious, Mr. Speaker, but I can assure you it is germane in the light of new evidence. In view of the fact there are more than 300 slaughterhouses in Quebec which are not under federal inspection or any inspection, and given the fact that the federal government knew as far back as 1968 that meat unfit for human consumption was being sold for human consumption-the evidence indicates that sales had reached massive proportions by 1973-did the hon. gentleman's department inform the government of Quebec of its suspicions and, in particular, did it inform the Attorney General of Canada what was taking place with a view to proceeding under the Food and Drugs Act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: SALE OF TAINTED MEAT IN QUEBEC-INQUIRY WHETHER FEDERAL DEPARTMENT INFORMED QUEBEC OR ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA OF SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only repeat what I have always said in the House. It is always the same thing, it is quite clear, the facts have been established. I merely invite the hon. member to refer to the questions which have been

June 19, 1975

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to inform the House that the Department of Justice is commencing preparation of a miscellaneous statute law amendment bill. There are a number of unique features in both the nature of the proposed bill and the method by which we propose to develop its content. I will be commenting upon these later. However, I would like to start by pointing to some of the reasons we are proposing such a bill.
It is possible for law reform to proceed on a number of levels. Law reform can occur simply by the modification of procedures used in administering laws. It can also occur through judicial decisions. It is important that law reform not proceed in a narrow and shortsighted way and that its broadest ramifications be kept constantly in view. It is important that appropriate policies responsive to the needs of our citizens be embodied in legislation. Much of our discussion in this chamber revolves around the appropriateness of various policies in meeting these needs. In my opinion, law reform should proceed on all of these planes simultaneously. Naturally, it will proceed at varying rates at these different levels since each has its own mechanisms of acceleration and restraint.
But it is also important that law reform proceed at another level, it is important that our legislation be constantly pruned and trimmed, shorn of anachronisms and inconsistencies, and changed in areas of obvious inadequacy where there can be no disagreement amongst reasonable persons about the need for modification or the form such modification should take. Surprisingly enough, it is this kind of law reform which has in some ways fallen behind. One reason is that pressure upon House time often precludes amendments to a bill being introduced until 
major amendments occur. The housekeeping changes for a particular statute will then be included in a larger bill. When the bill is debated, the housekeeping changes usually receive quick approval from all parties. Meanwhile, desirable housekeeping changes for other statutes which would in all likelihood also receive quick approval from all parties must remain dormant for a number of years until their particular statute is ripe for amendments of a major nature.
We propose, therefore, to provide a vehicle for proceeding with legislation of a non-controversial character. I stress the phrase "non-controversial" since it will be the main criterion by which proposals for inclusion in the bill will be assessed. Determination of the criterion will not be difficult to establish. A proposal would become controversial as soon as one of the parties expressed opposition to it. In such a situation, the proposal would be rejected and would no longer be considered for inclusion in the bill.
In other words, the bill will only include provisions about which we can reach quick and easy agreement. Proposals for inclusion in the bill will be invited from every member of the House and we will welcome all of these for consideration. In addition, we propose to make a comprehensive examination of federal statutes and to invite members of the bar, judges and others who are directly affected by federal legislation to offer proposals for inclusion in the bill.
I envisage a completely open process in developing the bill. I see the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs playing a particularly active role in this connection, and Department of Justice officials would be fully accessible to the committee. Indeed, after consideration and approval of the subject matter by the, cabinet, we propose to refer the subject matter of the bill to this committee for final approval before the bill is introduced.
I am sure that most hon. members can think of obviously desirable changes in legislation which they would like to see. The work of the Standing Committee on Statutory Instruments might well generate suggestions with respect to some of the regulation-making powers. Any admend-ments at all could be included provided they can meet the test of being non-controversial as described previously. Money clauses would not as a rule be included.
We would hope to see the first bill introduced within a year and to see subsequent bills of this nature on an annual basis.

Mr. Speaker, the proposed legislation is I think an exciting experience, controversy being the very basis of our parliamentary system. That does not prevent one from witnessing frequent examples of co-operation and goodwill in Parliament.
This bill will give members of all parties in the House an opportunity to participate in the improvement of Canadian legislation in a direct and non-partisan way. Its sucess will depend on the co-operation of each and everyone. I am sure this mechanism will be a true service to the Canadian people and I am anxious 'to discuss it in more detail with the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
June 19, 1975

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have grave doubts whether the minister should have taken the time of the House to make this announcement and to impinge upon the time of a motion by the opposition. About five years ago the Law Reform Commission was set up to recommend changes in the law, but we have not seen any legislation resulting from the many studies and reports the commission has made. It is time the people of Canada were provided with legislation of substance to deal with some of the important matters confronting us today: the questions of gun control, abortion, capital punishment, and new approaches taken to conviction and sentence with regard to people who have been convicted. These are some of the issues and I would have been happy if the minister had said he will introduce legislation with regard to them.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has told the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs that before he introduces the new young offenders bill he will circulate it to the members of the committee, and it seems to me that
Law Reform
the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) on various occasions in the last few months has said he intends to bring forth an omnibus bill with regard to amendments to the Criminal Code. I think he should take the same approach as the Solicitor General and at this time circulate proposed amendments concerning the subjects with which he hopes to deal.
I hope that he will deal with gun control, abortion and capital punishment. These are vital issues affecting the Canadian people. To come forth this afternoon with a housekeeping bill on which he says his department is working and hopes to prepare within a year is a very disappointing statement by the minister. Surely we can all agree that housekeeping amendments are necessary and it is necessary to have the input of judges, lawyers and others who are directly affected by it. I am certain he will get co-operation with respect to that type of legislation.

The simple test the minister puts with regard to the "non-controversial" aspect-that is, if it is non-controversial he will put it in the legislation some time later-is a cop-out with regard to his duties and obligations. The minister has to deal with some of the problems Canadian people are facing today. Instead of saying, "I am going to bring forth a housekeeping bill", he should say, "I am going to bring forth amendements to the Criminal Code". He should take the same approach as the Solicitor General and circulate the bill, so that people directly affected by it can study it during the summer and be ready for debate in the fall. That would be a better approach.
Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed in the Minister of Justice. I think he is capable of better things, and this is certainly not worthy of him.

management of Air Canada advises as follows: 1. Between November 1, 1974 and April 29, 1975, four pressurization decreases occurred. During this period, the company's 53 DC-9s completed 66,508 flights, for a rate of one incident for every 16,700 flights.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
That this House declares that Canada has a special right to manage and harvest the living resources on and over its continental shelf and slope and must act immediately to assert her right to manage and control those resources.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should point out at the outset that the motion was drafted in such a way as to not question the confidence of the government. It is not a no confidence motion but, rather, seeks the views of members of the House of Commons on a very important matter.
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today involved what is without a doubt the single most important issue facing a large segment of the population of the country, particularly those living in the Atlantic provinces and British Columbia. For the people of my province it is a matter of survival, because despite its ups and downs the fishing industry continues to be the most important factor in the economy of Newfoundland and exerts by far the greatest influence on the social and economic fabric of our communities and our people. The province of Newfoundland is not alone in that regard. The fishing industry is equally important to other regions of this country. I am sure my colleagues from the other regions will be outlining in some detail the importance of the industry to their respective provinces in the course of this debate.
The fishery resources upon which our fishermen on both the east and west coasts depend are not only important for their economic survival but also their way of life, which is being seriously threatened and indeed is facing total collapse unless immediate action is taken by this government. Given the fact that this situation and the resultant social and economic problems are a direct result of overfishing on the part of foreign fishing fleets operating off our coasts, it is imperative that Canada immediately begin, in a determined and meaningful way, the process of exercising sovereign rights over our continental shelf for the purpose of enabling this country to properly manage, harvest and rehabilitate our fishery resources.
Surely by this time, Madam Speaker, with all the scientific data that is available and with the rapid decline in fish landings despite our increased effort and capability, this government must realize the need for immediate action. It must realize, too, that attempts to regulate international fisheries by international law have been notoriously long drawn-out and singulary unsuccessful. The Geneva Law of the Sea conference was a devastating example of the weakness of such a conference for the solution of international fisheries problems of a pressing nature. We were optimistic, to say the least, to expect 150 countries, each with dozens of individual concerns, to agree to a single treaty containing over 300 separate articles and covering such a wide range of issues.
We must recognize, also, that most nations of the world are not compelled, as Canada is, to an early solution of Law of the Sea problems. They do not have to contend

with a rapidly declining fishery, and for the most part they have no other vital marine interests which urgently require protection by a new legal regime such as that sought by Canada at the Geneva conference.
We must bear in mind the failure of past Law of the Sea Conferences to negotiate a meaningful treaty. Madam Speaker, there is no guarantee, therefore, that even a further session in 1976 will necessarily end in the signing of a treaty. Even if it did, its ratification, the passage of necessary legislation, establishment of management mechanism and even a rapid phase-down of foreign fishing effort would add years to a process which by that time would have lost its rationale because of the long past decline of fish stocks, fishermen and the social fabric of our coastal fishing communities.
It is obvious, therefore, that if we are to avert the total collapse of this country's fishing industry, of the very social and economic existence of a large number of our people, unilateral action is the only option open to this government. Such action would provide a clearcut indication of Canada's determination to manage, control and rehabilitate, where necessary, our fish stocks. I ask this question, Madam Speaker: What other course of action is open to us? The Geneva Law of the Sea Conference and other similar conferences dating back to 1958 failed miserably in attempts to achieve a solution of this problem. We are running out of time; our fish stocks are being dangerously depleted.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet ought to study the history of the fisheries of Newfoundland and learn how our ancestors fared in international fishery matters. I think it would be instructive if they could learn the progress Newfoundland made in asserting and defending her rights to the marine resources around her coast. All these rights were acquired through unilateral action.
Newfoundland made her first initiative to protect her fisheries in 1857; she made that initiative in the international arena just two years after the colony had been granted responsible government. Faced with an English government which persisted in paying more attention to that country's good relations with more powerful and prestigious European countries than to Newfoundland's interest-and Newfoundland's interest lay in resisting the claims of certain countries to fishing rights off Newfoundland's coast-the Newfoundland legislature of that time passed a resolution similar to the one we are debating here today. At the same time it condemned the actions of the English government for trading off Newfoundland's territorial and maritime rights without the consent of the legislature.
In the end, the English government backed down and admitted that "the rights enjoyed by the colony of Newfoundland are not to be ceded or exchanged without their consent." Subsequently, in the latter part of the nineteenth century when dealing with American, Canadian and French vessels fishing inside her territorial waters, Newfoundland pulled no punches. The famous Bait Act, the equivalent of closing the ports today to foreign vessels, and our fishing regulations generally were enforced with a
June 19, 1975

severity which made the hair stand on the heads of English diplomats and did little to endear Newfoundland to the ballroom sets of London and other European capitals.
In 1904 the fisheries protection service of Newfoundland had under its jurisdiction five cruisers. These, equipped with the necessary hardware, set out to enforce our country's fishing regulations-and enforce them they did. The record shows that in one year, seven foreign fishing vessels were arrested and convicted for offences such as fishing within our territorial waters, throwing fish offal overboard on the fishing grounds, and larceny of a fleet's herring nets and gear. I ask, what action has this country taken to protect our marine resources? What action has this country, with a population exceeding 20 million people, taken? Consider what Newfoundland, with a population of a mere 250,000 people, did 75 years ago. The people of the province acted out of conviction and put their money where their mouth was, as it were.
A few years later, in 1910, a special international arbitration board established between England and the United States confirmed that Newfoundland and Canada were justified in using headland to headland base lines from which to measure their territorial seas. England later succeeded in persuading Canada to forgo the headland to headland concept and, instead, to accept a ten-mile maximum for closing lines across her bays. This, of course, was a complete distortion of the arbitration board's ruling and in the case of Newfoundland would have reduced drastically the area under Newfoundland's control. Newfoundland, consequently, refused to accept the proposition put forward and, subsequently, declared unilaterally her right to establish a headland to headland base line which continued up to confederation and was agreed to by Canada when Newfoundland entered confederation in 1949.
So you see, Madam Speaker, we eastern Canadians, among whom I include Newfoundlanders, never took too kindly to having our fishery resources plundered by foreign nations. What is more important, our people were prepared to fight for and defend our rights to those resources before confederation. Of course, after confederation that responsibility was vested in the Canadian government. If the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is interested in Newfie jokes, let him try that one on for size. The real lesson, Madam Speaker, lies not in nostalgia; it lies in recognizing that a people's will, a will to stand strong, united and determined against the encroachments of major powers once protected our vital interests. It can do this again.
This government's willingness or otherwise to protect our fish stocks must be looked at in the context of how economically weak regions of this country are treated generally. Obviously, fishing rights are irrelevant to the maintenance of the economic and social fabric of our more wealthy landlocked provinces. As these provinces hold the balance of power politically and economically, is it any wonder that Ottawa has failed to appreciate our problems and refuses to act in our better interests?
Newfoundlanders have not forgotten the lesssons of the past. They have not forgotten what happened when we were a colony of Great Britain, when that country sacrificed our fisheries because it was unwilling to prejudice its international relations with other more powerful and pre-
National Resources
stigious European countries. If these words have a familiar ring, the reason is that it has become increasingly obvious that the present government has adopted a similar attitude. Our fishermen would be naive indeed if they did not recognize the real reason for the government's unwillingness to take unilateral action and protect their livelihood and way of life. Unfortunately, our government are more concerned with maintaining their Mr. Clean image abroad, their Mr. Nice Guy image, than with solving the problems of our fishermen.
There are times when government members talk really tough-times like a few weeks before an election. For example, at a Liberal rally in Corner Brook, Newfoundland, on June 24, 1974, a mere 14 days before the July 8 federal election, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson)-the member for that great fishing constituency, Burin-Burgeo-got really tough. Apparently he was willing to take on all the ICNAF countries and all other countries which fish off our coasts, singlehandedly, and whip the daylights out of them. Let me quote what he said at that meeting:
Canada unilaterally will take control of the continental shelf off its coasts if current Law of the Sea negotiations do not go mostly her way.
The minister, then wearing the hat of a candidate seeking re-election in Burin-Burgeo, which happens to be more dependent on the fishery than any other federal constituency in Canada, went on to say:
Canada does not want to enter the Law of the Sea conference in Caracas with a big stick. If it all comes apart at the seams we simply can't leave matters as they stand.
The minister concluded his speech by saying:
Canada must have control over fisheries on the continental shelf and if Canada cannot negotiate control over the shelf and their immense fishery resources, it will have no choice but to take unilateral action.
I should mention as well that the Prime Minister attended the same rally in Cornerbrook on that day. His great contribution to the problem facing our fishermen and to alleviating their anxiety for the future was an assurance that the Law of the Sea conference would accept the Canadian position, that of a 200-mile exclusive fishing zone. I ought to mention that the conference in which the Prime Minister expressed such overwhelming confidence was the one which was held in Caracas in 1974. That conference failed to produce a treaty. Since then another conference has been held in Geneva and it, too, failed to negotiate a convention for the protection of our marine resources.
The question we have to ask ourselves, particularly those of us who live in the Atlantic area or on the west coast of this country, is: How much longer can we wait? How many more conferences must, we have before the Prime Minister, the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) get the message and act to protect our fishing industry and our fishermen?
This government is obviously hung up on conferences. There have been conferences since 1958. Already plans are being made for another conference in New York in 1976. We are rapidly developing an elite corps of conference-

June 19, 1975
National Resources
goers. Maybe it can be arranged to have the New York conference coincide with the World Series.

At least something would be
accomplished.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
If this keeps up, we will have more conference-goers than we will have fishermen. The latest conference, the one in which the government is now asking the fishermen to place their faith and hopes, is the ICNAF conference currently being held in Edinburgh, Scotland. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and his colleague, the Minister of State (Fisheries), have courageously instructed their officials attending the meeting that Canada will settle for nothing less than a 40 per cent reduction in the fishing effort of the 14 member nations of ICNAF. Failing to agree to such a proposition will result, they say, in the closing of our east coast ports to all foreign fishing ships.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that they are asking for a 40 per cent reduction in the fishing effort and not in the fish quotas and, as I will point out later, therein lies the gimmick. The minister's threat to close our east coast ports must have caused some sleepless nights in the countries concerned, particularly in Russia, Poland and East and West Germany, all of which are major plunderers of our marine resources and have been guilty of violating the existing ICNAF quotas. Ships operated by these countries have no real need to visit our ports because they can be fully serviced at sea. As far as the other countries are concerned, it would simply be a matter of diverting their fishing ships to the French- islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon where they would be welcomed with open arms.
Now a word about the ICNAF meetings and our government's demand for a 40 per cent reduction in the fishing effort of the member nations. I am sure the Minister of State (Fisheries) realizes that even if the ICNAF meeting does produce an agreement for a 40 per cent reduction in effort, it is quite conceivable that such an agreement would not lessen by one pound the quantity of fish caught in the ICNAF fishing zone. This government has proven itself incapable of adequately policing the ICNAF quotas. Not long ago the minister told the committee that the Russians were caught violating their agreed quotas on caplin. I think the minister was being quite conservative when he said their quotas were exceeded by a small number. I was told by a reliable source that they exceeded their quotas by five times. This is the type of thing that is going on in the ICNAF areas. It is certainly one we have to guard against.
If the government is incapable of policing the ICNAF quotas where men can physically go on board a ship and see the amount of fish in the holds, how can we expect them to properly police an agreement to reduce a fishing effort? It would mean men on every ship, working around the clock counting nets, counting the hours they are in the water, counting the number of times they are hauled, assessing the workload of the crew members and the amount of effort they are putting into their work. It would be an impossible task. I do not think the Minister of State (Fisheries) and his colleagues are serious about it. Such a proposition is ridiculous because it would be impossible to enforce.

I shall outline, for the record, the situation as it now exists with respect to fishing activity in the ICNAF convention areas by its member nations. These are official Government of Canada statistics. In 1960, Canada's total groundfish catch was 723,000 metric tons, as opposed to
885,000	metric tons in 1973; an increase of 22.4 per cent. The same year, Russia's total catch was 258,000 metric tons, and in 1973 1,354,000 metric tons, which is an increase of 424.8 per cent. In 1960, the United States caught 477,000 metric tons, against 971,000 metric tons in 1973; an increase of 103.6 per cent. Spain, in 1960, took 177,000 metric tons and in 1973 its catch had amounted to 238,000 metric tons; an increase of 34.5 per cent. In 1960, Poland caught 4,000 metric tons and in 1973 their catches amounted to 267,000 metric tons, which is an increase of 6,575 per cent. The increases in the catches of the other member nations of the ICNAF convention are equally as glaring as those to which I have referred.
To sum up, the grand total of groundfish caught in the ICNAF area in 1973 is exactly double the tonnage caught in 1960. I should point out, also, that in 1974 the total fish landings in Newfoundland, under all headings, was less than one-half that in 1969, just five years earlier, despite our increased fishing effort and capability. Is it any wonder that we have lost faith in ICNAF and in this government?
The fishermen of this country are facing a bleak future. Their means of survival are being plundered by foreign interests and their government continues to treat the problem with total indifference. Newfoundland's representative to the Law of the Sea conference, Mr. Cabot Martin, has very appropriately summed up the situation in which we now find ourselves. Canadian fishermen, he said, should ask themselves why the dangers of unilateralism are acceptable to Ottawa when it comes to saving polar bears, but not when it comes to the very survival of our fishing areas as communities. Of course, the same can be said with regard to seals. The government is more interested in preserving our seal heads and, to some extent, taking unilateral action than in taking action to protect a way of life enjoyed by a large number of Canadians in the Atlantic area and on the west coast of this country.
As far as Newfoundland is concerned, we are at the crossroads in our history as a province of Canada. Our people are not content to remain poor relatives of the Upper Canadian-oriented bureaucracy. They will no longer be satisfied with just the provision of the necessary public services and other fringe benefits doled out by Ottawa to the weaker provinces. We did not relinquish 400 years of independence to become an economically deprived province of Canada. We demand that the central bureaucracy go much further than just keeping us alive. We demand the right to be given the means to develop our natural resources and preserve our society and our way of life according to our own priorities. If we are denied that right, the question which will inevitably follow is: Has confederation been worth while?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the House
June 19, 1975

and the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter) that I certainly accept his general objective and good intentions in putting his motion before the House today. The objective which members of the House are determined to achieve is that Canada be able to exercise exclusive and effective management rights over the living resources off its coasts. With this objective in mind, I certainly share the purposes of the hon. member.
I also share his appreciation of the serious situation which exists in our fisheries, particularly off the east coast. We have not attempted-I certainly have not attempted, nor has the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc)-to gloss over the fact that there is overfishing by foreign fleets or that this overfishing has resulted in a reduction in the level of stocks traditionally harvested by Canadian fishermen, for instance, cod, haddock and herring.
The hon. member has talked about the fishermen of his province. I could talk about the fishermen of the province of Nova Scotia. There is a rich fishery in Nova Scotia. It is not as rich as that of Newfoundland, but a large number of the citizens of that province depend upon the fishery and many of the most picturesque and appealing communities rely for their existence on a viable fishing industry. So we are all agreed as to the importance of this issue.
We know that the decline in stocks has resulted in financial hardship for fishing operators, for fishermen and for the industry as a whole. In response to the facts the hon. member has been putting before us this afternoon, we have taken measures-exceptional measures, in my view- to alleviate the hardship which has been caused, making available, for example, subsidies totalling $80 million. I am sure that in the course of this debate my colleague the Minister of State for Fisheries and others on this side of the House will be drawing attention to what the government has been doing to support the fishermen of the Atlantic coast.
Having reached this stage in my speech, I am afraid I begin to differ from the hon. member for St. John's West. I invite hon. members to read the motion we are asked to support. It states:
-this House declares that Canada has a special right to manage and harvest the living resources on and over its continental shelf and slope and must act immediately to assert her right to manage and control those resources.
The motion calls for the exercise of a special right over the living resources on and over the continental shelf and slope. Mr. Speaker, I believe the motion is seriously flawed and I cannot understand how an hon. member from British Columbia, such as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) whose name appears as seconder of the motion, could support it. In limiting our fishing zones to the continental shelf, as the motion does, the hon. member is limiting our claim on the Pacific coast to 60 or 70 miles.

speechtext: This is the motion which the House of Commons is being asked to declare to the world. I wonder how the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich could ever go back to his fishermen and say, "In your case I settled for jurisdiction extending 60 or 70 miles, though the Canadian position at the present time at the Law of the Sea conference represents at least a search for a 200-mile economic zone, with certain preferential rights related to the species of fish which exist immediately beyond the 200-mile economic zone itself.".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext: What about the continental shelf?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
When it comes to the east coast, the hon. member has done the very opposite of what he has proposed for the west coast. We have been arguing at the Law of the Sea conference-and we understood that we were supported in this argument by members on the other side of the House-that a 200-mile economic zone is our objective and that we would seek exclusive management rights for species that exist within the boundary of 200 miles. That has been the policy we have put forward.
The Canadian parliament is now being asked to tell the world that we are seeking not only a 200-mile zone plus the exclusive management rights to which I have referred, but also jurisdiction on the high seas to 400 miles and 600 miles. I wonder whether members on the other side of the House have seriously considered the effect this kind of resolution would have on the position that has been taken by Canadian negotiators at the Law of the Sea conference up to the present time.
As it is written, it is not difficult for me or for any member of the House to vote against the motion. I would think that unless hon. members opposite want to create great difficulties and wrong impressions they ought, after the debate has taken place, to agree to withdraw the motion and not have a large group of their party support this kind of distortion of what up to the present has been Canadian policy. I did not write the motion but I have read it, and what I have said to the House is what its

June 19, 1975
National Resources
words mean. I have to deal with the motion, not with what is in the mind of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich.
Apart from these defects existing in the motion, the hon. member is asking for unilateral action now for establishing a zone of 600 miles on the Atlantic coast and 70 miles on the Pacific coast. If I may put that incredible proposition aside, let me turn to a more achievable objective, namely, unilateral action to achieve the 200-miles economic zone itself. What are the implications of that particular action at the present time? First of all, Canada would have to enforce, at short notice, its new jurisdiction against the fleets of other nations. Hon. members know that international law as it presently stands gives all states, including these other nations, the right to harvest freely the living resources of the high seas; that is, in the area immediately beyond the territorial sea of a coastal state.
At the present time, under international law-we are trying vigorously at the Law of the Sea conference to change the present international law-a coastal state has no right to an exclusive fishing zone beyond its territorial sea. We are totally dissatisfied with that international law governing the fisheries and we are doing, and will continue to do, our utmost to change it. It is clear that, in the absence of detailed negotiations and agreements with other member states now fishing in these waters, to declare unilateral action today would involve us in serious confrontation. The hon. member has no assurance, unless these negotiations do take place and mutual accommodations are reached, that vessels would recognize our declaration instead of preferring to recognize existing international law.
I realize the attractiveness of making resounding statements about taking unilateral action now, but I also believe it is necessary to explain to the fishermen what the implications may be in the long run and to explain to them that there are hazards in this direction as well. It may be that after careful analysis it is decided that unilateral action may not bring results any faster than working through the multilateral approach that we have worked within and which we have regarded as the preferred solution.
Then I ask hon. members to reflect on two other points. By voting for unilateral action, this House votes for unilateral action today. What effect would that have on Canada's objective of reaching agreement at the Law of the Sea conference on the coastal states' preferential rights to the living resources in the area of and beyond the 200 miles? If we change the hon. member's motion to make it conform to a more realistic objective, namely, a 200-mile economic zone, and if we declare it today through this parliament, what effect would that have on the preferential rights that we are seeking for those species that exist adjacent to the boundaries of the 200 miles?
What effect would it have, I ask the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, on the special regime that we have been seeking for salmon, a special regime giving the state of origin exclusive management rights and imposing a ban on high seas fishing of these species? We know perfectly well that that particular regime for salmon, so vital on the Pacific and on the Atlantic, can only come about as a result of a multilateral treaty. Would we be justified today, without negotiation, without consultation with any 
other member state, in jeopardizing the objective that we are patiently reaching in our negotiations of establishing a regime for the salmon?
It should be obvious to hon. members that the state of origin by itself, without the agreement of other interested parties, would be powerless to exercise effective control over salmon throughout its migratory range. That has been one of the constant concerns that I have had in considering the prospect of unilateral action. What will it do for the 200-mile zone? What will it do for preferential rights adjacent to the 200-mile economic zone? What will it do for the salmon? In proposing such unilateral action we cannot overlook other important objectives that Canada has in mind at the Law of the Sea conference. The continental margin and the protection of the marine environment, all of these are part of the total package which Canada is seeking. What effect would unilateral action today have on these other objectives? It seems to me that we have to consider all these facts before we launch forward and follow the well intentioned advice of the hon. member for St. John's West.
We have been working at the Law of the Sea conference and I disagree entirely with the hon. member's analysis of that conference. I believe that while it has not resulted in instant international law on fisheries, it has made great achievements. Our fisheries objectives at that conference are well known. They are, first of all exclusive management rights to the coastal state over the living resources within the 200-mile zone, preferential rights over stocks occurring in the area immediately beyond the 200-mile limit, and exclusive management rights over salmon stocks throughout their migratory range. These objectives were not put into international law at the last Law of the Sea conference but it did result in the production of a negotiating text in which these issues went very far in in reflecting Canadian interests.
Yesterday the minister from Norway was in Ottawa. Mr. Evensen and his group were very active at the conference, under his leadership, in working on a fisheries text and other texts. It is a fact that his work and his texts have almost totally been reflected in the single negotiating text. This is a negotiating text, not a settlement and not a negotiated text; but it is of interest to us that the main objectives of Canada have been achieved, with the exception that the preferential rights we are seeking for species adjacent to the 200-mile economic zone have been dealt with only vaguely.
I was particularly delighted, when the text was tabled, to see how the regime for salmon had been reflected in that text. This text would recognize the primary responsibility and interest of the state of origin in respect of salmon spawned in its rivers. There again, the state of origin would be entitled to set the total allowable catch for its salmon stocks. Still another provision would prohibit fishing for salmon beyond the 200-mile limit, with allowances made for some accommodation of existing high seas fisheries. As the hon. member knows, such fisheries have been conducted only by Japan which has taken some mainly of U.S. and U.S.S.R. origin both within and beyond 200 miles from land. In addition to that, the single text would close the door to new states interested in fishing
June 19, 1975

salmon in the high seas beyond 200 miles. Finally, the salmon article of the single negotiating text would enjoin an adjacent state in whose exclusive 200-mile fishing zone salmon would migrate to agree with the state of origin on conservation and management measures.
I have already stated that the single negotiating text does not adequately reflect our objective in respect of coastal state preferential rights over fish stocks occurring immediately adjacent to the 200-mile limit. In putting these points before the House, I think we have every reason to register satisfaction with the degree of progress made in the fisheries situation itself. If we could translate these objectives immediately into international law, this subject certainly would not be debated today.
We are now faced with a number of points the government must deal with before it can possibly implement the declaration of unilateral action. First of all, we have to consult with other countries such as Norway and the United States which may be interested in working along with us in achieving fisheries objectives. That is essential. It is essential, also, for us to assess fully the results of the efforts being made by the Minister of State for Fisheries at the ICNAF conference. Canada has taken bold initiatives at this conference with a view to seeking agreement on a substantial reduction of foreign fishing effort of groundfish stocks, with appropriate reductions in quota allocations to foreign fishing fleets.

speechtext: That is only a scientific conference.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
That is a scientific conference with very important implications for reaching our objectives. In fact, in reply to the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), let me tell him that I was advised by fisheries representatives that if we could achieve our objectives at ICNAF, the concern for immediate unilateral action would be considerably reduced, if not eliminated. We have had a final meeting in Edinburgh, and I listened this morning to Dr. Needier telling us it is now proposed to have an additional meeting in September to follow up the ICNAF studies.
Finally, there is the question of the fishing fleets which are now fishing in these waters-waters which are high seas and in which they may fish under present international law. It seems to me it would be prudent for Canada to assess very carefully the attitude of these countries and to conduct negotiations with them before we accepted a motion such as the one put forward today by the hon. member for St. John's West. I would prefer to administer a long-term policy that would get results in fisheries rather than yield to pressure to declare unilateral action instantaneously, the benefits of which may not arrive for quite some time unless the ground work is carefully laid.
As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, I share the concern of the hon. member but I think the wording of his motion, if accepted, would get us into great difficulties. The hon. member's motion would treat the west coast differently from the east coast: it would declare a jurisdiction of 60 or 70 miles off the west coast and a jurisdiction of 400 to 600 miles for fisheries off the Atlantic coast. If accepted, this would cause us great difficulty and would distort beyond recognition present Canadian policy which has been accepted on all sides of the House.
National Resources
Furthermore, there are other steps we have to take in conjunction with continuing sessions on the Law of the Sea. One step is the ICNAF operation, another is consultation with states fishing in our waters and another is consultation with states like Norway which have similar fisheries objectives.
I want to conclude by saying, as I said at the Law of the Sea conference at Caracas and again at Geneva, that there is a point at which Canada would consider, as one of its options, a unilateral declaration. We have always maintained that as one of our options. We continue to maintain it, but we think to take it today would be against Canada's best interests.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I make a point of participating for a few moments in this debate on the motion relating to fisheries.
The motion we are now discussing provides us with the opportunity to express our views on that matter, which is of utmost importance. Furthermore, it is nothing new that members of this House ask the government to apply a policy serving the interests of our country and fishermen.
Madam Speaker, the principle underlying the motion before the House today is to provide Canada with a special legislation enabling us to manage and develop marine wildlife and flora resources in the waters of our continental shelf and slopes, and also to allow this country to take immediate action to assert its right to manage and control those resources.
It is quite obvious that a country like ours that has immense openings on the Pacific and the Atlantic needs legislation that can guarantee not only autonomy but also-and this is extremely important-respect for our fishing rights along its coasts so it will be really possible to apply them. So we must take the necessary steps to protect our resources because in face of their depletion one cannot remain quiet or indifferent. As a matter of fact, the motion now before us deals with a question that has been of tremendous importance for a very long time already, particularly for the economic life and the well-being of the Canadian people.
More than ever in the past the question of the use of sea resources is crucial, considering the recent discoveries that allow to assess in part the tremendous possibilities represented by the potential development of oil and other minerals that lie at the bottom of the ocean. In that respect I am more convinced than ever following a recent visit in the territories of northern Canada about the wealth of resources in the subsoil and even in the sea, resources that have remained undeveloped but are there nevertheless for all Canadians.
I was very surprised to discover the immense and tremendous resources that accumulate with the permission and under the authority of the government and also with the participation of the various companies interested in carrying out research and making greater use of the resources in those territories.
Of course, there as in all other fields of economic activity, countries do not all enjoy the same natural advantages
29S76-25

June 19, 1975
National Resources
such as access to the sea and the existence of coastal areas. I admit quite readily for my part that our country is particularly well off. Indeed, in the east we have access to the Atlantic ocean, in the west the Pacific ocean, and in the north we touch the Arctic ocean, and that is fantastic.
Madam Speaker, we are quite aware of all our advantages. We also know that Canada has a very long coastal area that surrounds the country on three sides. For that reason, we are particularly concerned by the problem raised by the motion introduced this afternoon. The problem of sovereignty of a country over its surrounding coastal areas is not new. However, it is certain that the discovery of enormous mineral resources as well as the outstanding increase in the demand for sea products such as fish, for example, make it urgent to determine a course of conduct that will have to be accepted not only by Canada but also by all countries of the international community.
Madam Speaker, last March my colleague the member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) had the honour to attend the Law of the Sea Conference held in Geneva. I wish to point out that he gave us a report on that conference which was a very stimulating and rewarding experience.
According to some delegates, that conference was considered as the most important since the one held in San Francisco where the charter of the United Nations was drafted. The object of the last conference was to try to develop a marine constitution acceptable to all countries as a binding treaty. The problems discussed were quite complex. Among various issues discussed was the width of the continental shelf over which a coastal state would have sovereign rights for the exploration and development of resources and reference was also made to the delimitation of the marine ground which does not come under national jurisdiction and must ultimately be used for pacific purposes as the common inheritance of mankind.
We thought and still think that the best way to ensure a judicious use of ocean resources in the best interest of the world population would be a basic reform of maritime law that would give to the country full sovereignty over a zone extending 200 miles from its coasts and sometimes even to the limits of the continental shelf, depending on the location.
I sincerely believe that this is the only approach offering actual guarantees regarding the safeguard of sea resources. And the fact of giving to every coastal state the responsibility for, the sovereignty over and the property of resources in a zone extending 200 miles from the coasts is the only way to ensure good management and good allocation of those resources.
I for one think that if coastal zones belonged to everybody, in fact they would belong to no one and such a decision could result in an irrational pillage of resources. On the other hand, if every nation had full control over a coastal zone extending 200 miles offshore, each one of these nations would then have the responsibility to protect, develop and ensure good use of the resources under its jurisdiction.
Madam Speaker, I entirely understand the fear of the countries without coastal zones and that do not have

access to the sea, but I firmly believe that the interest of those countries lies, like for the others, in a responsible use of sea resources. On the other hand, it is undeniable that such a responsible use of resources is only possible if they are under national jurisdiction. Some countries might be worried by this position, but it is not difficult to set their mind at ease because I sincerely believe that they just have to recall the usual generosity of Canada towards them.
To claim that our country has contributed more than any other to the progress of developing countries with regard to natural resources and their use is in no way pretentious. Madam Speaker, as far as foreign aid is concerned, Canada ranks among the first in the world through the amounts of money it has given to help underdeveloped countries. CIDA's latest budget proves it. If we extend our jurisdiction over our coastal waters to a distance of 200 miles offshore, we will then be able to guarantee the protection and the reasonable use of the tremendous resources placed under our control, because, above all else, we will want to manage those resources justly, fairly, not only from the Canadian point of view, but also from that of the countries which can benefit from the advantages of that untold wealth which, if it is protected, conserved and well developed, can be of benefit to all humanity.
Madam Speaker, I am not saying anything new when I say that it is only since the period between the two world wars that a start has been made in the formulation of concepts that reflect the fundamental economic interests of the states endowed with coastal waters with regard to the fishing rights on the continental shelf; for the last 300 years, the law of the sea had reflected solely colonial, military and commercial interests. It became obvious that international law was growing less and less adapted to the problems and needs created out of technological progress. This seems fairly obvious to me when we allude, for instance, to the marine environment; when we speak of it, we must consider not only water pollution but also the fishing industry.
I remember well, Madam Speaker, when, at the time of a conference attended by the Canadian members of parliament and the members of the French National Assembly, the important matter of the pollution of the Arctic ocean was made the topic of a detailed study and the adoption of very serious resolutions through which interested countries were asked to take part in a comprehensive study, with a view to avoiding water pollution in that vast territory, which shows once more how important this question is. That is why I feel our neighbour to the south and all the countries in the vicinity of this vast territory would be well advised to support our country in its efforts to preserve this immense territory which I think will serve future generations as a very important reserve for drinking water and fish products.
If there is something we must realize, it is that only since Canada has taken a number of initiatives in the area of environmental protection of the sea has the law of the sea finally taken these matters into account. As a matter of fact, it is quite easy to see that the freedom of the high seas concept has been abused to such a point that it condones excessive fishing as well as pollution.
June 19, 1975

Well, we should not live in these vast territories as though no human beings were to live there after us. We must realize that there will be future generations and that it is our duty to adopt legislation to protect these vast territories which, if we do our job well and assume our responsibilities, will serve future generations as an immense reserve of various products to meet their needs. This way we shall be protecting the general interests of our country and not those of a limited few, following guidelines which should help protect the interest of the community.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, it goes without saying that we should have, as a coastal state, the right to defend our interests in this area. We all know that fishing in the Gulf of St. Lawrence is forbidden to foreign fleets and that many other steps and initiatives have been taken by the government, as evidence of its interest in fisheries. Parliament also should support the efforts which are made now to assure more thorough and complete supervision over this area.
The interest shown by the government in that field seems very normal to me if we think that the fishing industry is vitally important on our east and west coasts, not only economically but also socially and humanly. It is anyway for the Canadian people, since a great many Canadians depend on this industry for their living, either in the fishing or the marketing field. The fishing industry creates many jobs across Canada, and at the same time enables Canadians to add fish to their diet, which is highly recommended by medical authorities. It is also a sector of the Canadian economy which has to be protected and developed if we want fishermen to have a reasonable income which will allow them to face the future with confidence.
That is why, Madam Speaker, I urge the government to do its utmost to guarantee the full protection and recognition of the richness of marine life in Canada. Those are the remarks I wanted to make sincerely, during the discussion of this motion, to support strongly, as a Canadian and as a responsible parliamentarian, the effort that is being made and that will have to be made in the future to protect this industry and our coasts from the invasion of foreign countries.
