speechtext:
I can understand the wording of the motion as it is, but the point is valid that it does not cover the 200-mile zone respecting the west coast fisheries; my amendment will cover that point.
On the subject of a unilateral declaration, the first charge that those of us who support it have to answer is that it is a departure from Canada's traditional role as a broker in international affairs and a departure from her traditional support of international agreements. In fact, Mr. Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth. At the Law of the Sea conference, two-thirds of all states and 90 per cent of the world's population agreed with Canada's position on the 200-mile zone. The unilateral declaration does not harm the consensus; in fact it will confirm what has become an accepted economic zone around the world.
The major reason for moving into a unilateral declaration now is that the depletion of the east coast fishing stock has been a great tragedy to people on that coast. I am not going to go into the depressing figures for the east coast fishery, but one example is that the herring catch is down by 90 per cent. As the minister of fisheries has said many times, fishermen cannot eat negotiating texts. Herring fishermen cannot wait forever for these stocks to be protected. I hope the minister will see fit to back his fine words with action.
The criticism from the Secretary of State for External Affairs is that because of the sensitivity of the ICNAF conference and the delicate negotiations taking place, to move now would disturb those negotiations. In fact, I would suggest the reverse is true. You do not go into a poker game without all your cards. There is no reason why we should not move now, to support the position taken by the negotiator at the conference so that the countries concerned will know that Canada means business. I suggest that such caution at the ICNAF conference lessens our chances of getting the 40 per cent reduction which we seek. In fact, I would suggest that Canada's position will defeat the efforts of her representatives at the conference. There is every reason to believe we would be in a better position to save those stocks if we moved on a unilateral declaration.
International law on the subject of economic zones has always been developed in stages, by custom. We can go back to the case of the old Norwegian coast, which was probably the beginning of changes in boundaries in the world's oceans, when she decided the straight base line concept was the one she wished to adopt in order to define her territorial sea. Since then there have been the examples of Iceland and Peru. Each time there has been a declaration of this sort, I believe that international law has been advanced. The action taken by those countries has helped Canada to be successful in developing a consensus for the 200-mile zone. Surely we should go the last step; there is no reason why we should wait.
I want to deal with a problem raised by some of my friends who are world federalists, that Canada has somehow departed from her traditional role of support for world bodies. Dr. John Logue has described Canada's position as a moral monstrosity in terms of a unilateral declaration. That kind of elitist attitude, telling the group of 77 what is best for them, does no service at all to internationalism. In fact, it is the people in the developing
29576-25)4

June 19, 1975
National Resources
world who have supported Canada's concept of the 200-mile zone. They understand their own position and do not need to be lectured by someone like Dr. Logue. Countries of the Third World understand their own development and do not need to rely on some nebulous formula for the future.
I am not critical of Canada's conduct at the Law of the Sea conference, Madam Speaker. It is an enormous task to get 150 countries to agree to redraw the world's boundaries. The argument that we do not yet have a unilateral declaration does not destroy our success in developing a consensus; in fact, it encourages the consensus to be even more consolidated when the conference resumes in New York. Another aspect of the question of timing is the situation in the United States. Their Magnusson bill is still in the Senate and I believe it is supported by a legislator named Leggatt-obviously a very progressive legislator!

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
The United States is on the verge of moving to its economic zone. From my conversations with United States legislators I have been given to understand that the legislation should be in place by next fall and that they have sufficient votes in the House to override a presidential veto. I suppose Canada's position will then be: We can make our declaration now that the United States has again given the lead. I am asking that Canada show some leadership and not wait for the United States and Mexico to move on the economic zone. If we show leadership now, we will come out of the conference in much better shape.
I now want to say a few words about the west coast fishery. The largest salmon fishing river in the world runs through my riding. I might say that fishermen on the west coast are pleased at the development of the consensus concerning the 200-mile limit. It is interesting to note that fishermen on the west coast and on the east coast, despite all their differences, agree in their support for this motion-a motion which I propose to amend in a minute. Despite the differences in the fisheries, despite the difficulties involving high seas salmon fishing, the fishermen who actually work in the boats and pull in the fish see no merit in delaying any longer a unilateral declaration.
Some may argue that we risk losing salmon on the high seas unless a treaty is signed, but I submit that the risk is minimal. The treaty with the Japanese is such that almost no Canadian salmon are presently being taken by the Japanese. A unilateral declaration will satisfy and confirm the position of our fishermen, especially on the west coast. They think a 200-mile zone will do more to protect salmon than almost anything else even though they go out beyond the 200-mile zone. We are satisfied that Canada has enough levers on the high seas to protect high seas salmon even without an international treaty.
I want to say a word about the salmon enhancement program on the west coast. I have been a member of parliament since 1972, and it seems to me that every spring we hear the announcement concerning the salmon enhancement program. One looks forward to it much as one looks forward to the daffodils every year. We hear the

announcement concerning the salmon enhancement program, but unfortunately, like the daffodils, that promise seems to wither quickly and no action is taken on it. Perhaps the minister is following the old dictum: never carry out a political promise because you will lose it for the next election. Another dictum is: never spoil a good political promise with action.
I recall the previous minister of fisheries announcing the enhancement program. The figures quoted rise progressively, but I suppose that is owing to inflation. I do not suppose we shall see the latest estimated number of salmon in those spawning beds. I should like to see more action to develop our fisheries, action which the government has promised for a long time and to which our fishermen have been looking forward for a long time. The enhancement program makes for good press releases. Unfortunately, the press has a short memory; it forgets what was said last season about the enhancement program. If the Vancouver Sun people would read what happened last time the enhancement program was announced, they would see that this is not a new idea, that it is the same announcement each time and covers the same enhancement program. It is time to implement that excellent program which has been mentioned by this minister and his predecessor. It should be implemented regardless of the state of Canada-U.S. treaty negotiations. We cannot wait any longer to increase our salmon stocks.
If I may touch on the Law of the Sea concerning salmon, there are severe weaknesses in the unified draft treaty. I am talking about the one on which negotiations will be based at the New York conference. I hope the minister and his officials will take cognizance of these weaknesses. Article 54 (3)(b), which may be an attempt to limit high seas fishing, says:
The state of origin shall co-operate in minimizing economic dislocation in such other states fishing these stocks, taking into account the normal catch and the mode of operations-
On the surface, this looks like an attempt to keep the quantity of our salmon which foreign fleets catch about the same as it is now; it is an attempt to keep matters in their present position. I hope the minister's officials will look at the meaning of "economic dislocation." If the catch of some other species goes down, a country like Japan could well argue that it can increase the pressure on our salmon stocks to avoid economic dislocation. That is my tentative interpretation and I hope it is wrong. But I submit that the article as presently drafted leaves a serious loophole. The other part of the negotiated draft treaty which gives me concern is subparagraph (c) of article 54(3), which says:
States referred to in subparagraph (b), participating by agreement with the state of origin in measures to renew anadromous stocks, particularly by expenditures for that purpose, shall be given special consideration by the state of origin in the harvesting of stocks originating in its rivers.
I hope our negotiators remember the investment the United States made many years ago in Hell's Gate canyon. On the basis of . this investment the United States has been holding up negotiations for a long time. They want to make sure they get their proper share of the Fraser River catch. If this article is left as it is in the treaty, it will be thrown back at us every year in our negotiations with the United States. They will say, "We are simply confirming
June 19, 1975

the position that any foreign country which invests in Canadian fisheries is entitled forever to a share of those stocks." That is complete nonsense. The few dollars which the United States invested in Hell's Gate canyon many years ago represent about the best investment that country ever made, in terms of return. As I said, there is nothing wrong with a unilateral declaration now. The motion is timely. It will help us in our negotiations both on the east coast and on the west coast. It will help us with the U.S. salmon negotiations which as we know have been deferred for one year.
I wish to propose an amendment to the motion before the House in order to deal with the question raised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I raised this matter some time ago, by way of a motion under Standing Order 43, clearly calling for a 200-mile economic zone, or a zone out to the edge of the continental shelf, whichever is the greater. The intention was to protect our fisheries. With that in mind, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the word "slope", the following words:
or to the extent of a 200-mile economic zone, whichever is the
greater.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before anyone else intervenes, let me say to this House that I was at first shocked, then ashamed, subsequently disgusted and finally completely disappointed to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) descend to the depths of petty political ridicule. I say this because we brought forward the motion for two reasons, and they are significant. One is that this is an important motion for all of Canada, and the other is that it should haye all-party support.
We sought to frame a motion which could gather in all parties so that the government would know it had support from all sides of this House. The minister knows full well that the acceptance of this motion would not preclude action out to the 200-mile limit. He should be ashamed to suggest anything else. We simplified the motion so as to get within our net, if I can put it that way, the necessary minimum of jurisdiction and the widest possible support. To suggest otherwise is unworthy of a minister of the Crown.
The minister mentioned unilateral action. We deliberately avoided the word "unilateral". Wait until you hear what I am prepared to say, not what I had to prepare after hearing the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We deliberately avoided the word "unilateral" in order to show the government that it could count on the support of this House for some of its actions. We used the term "assert". It was chosen as a means of urging the government to back up its claims with enforcement capability. As I look at this, the ministry of fisheries wants the support
National Resources
of this House, because I do not think the government is giving it the full support it needs. Our argument is that we are not preparing now, as we ought to be, to enforce what we are claiming.
In his comments the minister seemed to operate on the theory that the incorporation or inclusion of a right or claim in a convention such as the claim to ownership of the salmon has the same value as automatic recognition by all nations in this world of that right or claim. The minister ought to know better than that. If I may be permitted to descend for a moment to the depths of political commentary which marked the minister's comments, I would say that to hold such a belief is a measure of the short length of time the minister has held his present office. The minister ought to know better. He knows that ICNAF is not being observed. Why does he think that because there is a right or claim in an international convention, the rest of the world is going to recognize it? They won't. You have to back it up. That is what we are trying to say. I hope the government wants the support of the House in that effort.
Conventions have to be supported with an adequate enforcement arsenal. That is the import of our motion today. These are areas of action where, surely, multi-party support is needed. Why do certain ministers strive without let-up to destroy or undermine that support by making a speech such as we heard today? It makes me see even more clearly the distinction I have always felt had to be made between a politician and a parliamentarian. The executive does not have a monopoly on the line to truth. They are, unless they are supremely ignorant and arrogant, capable of learning from others and being supported in some of their actions by other parties in this House. Is it because the executive wants full, entire and sole credit for any move it brings forward, any progress on the front being assailed? I wish to return to the comments I have prepared to show the support we are prepared to give the government in some of its activities.

Before continuing my comments on the issue of fisheries, which is so important for the Canadian economy, the welfare of several thousands of Canadians and the responsibilities of Canada in this area, I would like to express the gratitude of the Canadian people to the team of negotiators in Caracas and Geneva who, under the leadership of the eminent leader of the delegation, ambassador Allan Beesley, did such a good job in outlining the elements of maritime rights which are essential if Canada is to play its role in international affairs as concerns maritime problems.
The two conferences did not produce a drafted agreement which would only have had to be ratified. However, because of the negotiating ability so amply demonstrated by Mr. Beesley and his team, nothing was lost and much was gained in the sense that the credibility of Canada's position as concerns its claim is still intact. It was even possible to protect an ulterior position, which will allow us to establish jointly, or unilaterally in certain circumstances, conservation controls over certain parts of the continental shelf extending beyond the 200-nautical-mile zone which is generally recognized as the area of jurisdiction of coastal nations in certain respects. We are therefore grateful to Mr. Beesley and his team who have

June 19, 1975
National Resources
worked untiringly in our best interests, and I sincerely thank him for this.

I will give this government credit for pursuing these goals at Caracas, Geneva and elsewhere and supporting the untiring efforts of the Beesley team. However, I draw the line at the point which separates what we are prepared to seek or claim and what we are prepared to do to secure and defend. This is where we part company. If in the first area, that of claiming, the government has been active, the government has been negligent to the point of endangering our resources in the area of backing up those claims with an adequate policing and enforcing mechanism. No one can deny the importance of this second or implementation phase.
It is my impression that the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) is not as fully supported as he ought to be by his cabinet colleagues. It is the gap between profession and performance that concerns me. Ministers have said on many occasions in the House, in committee and over the air that we have adequate surveillance and can detect interlopers and poachers. I question even that: we are still awaiting decisions on some matters relating to our long-range patrol aircraft. Let us suppose we do. Who dares suggest that surveillance is to be equated with regulation and effective control? Surveillance merely means, in either of Canada's official languages, watching over-"veiller sur", "to stay up overnight," if you wish, "in order to watch over".
We have surveillance capability provided we get a replacement for the long-range patrol aircraft. We also have Telesat. We have it from the air, or from the stratosphere. However, I contend surveillance is not enough; there must be a real capability to track, pursue and if necessary to arrest those who refuse to observe the law, whether Canadian or international. This is the point the government seems unable to grasp. Is anyone here suggesting we ought to let the regime of lawlessness or disregard and disrespect for the law, which unfortunately now pervades dry land, be extended to the seas over which we are claiming jurisdiction? The government's performance suggests as much, because it steadfastly refuses to back up its claims with the means of enforcing its mandate over those claims once attained.
This neglect of enforcement capability is manifest in the failure of the government to establish and maintain a seagoing force commensurate with the area over which we hope to obtain jurisdiction. This was true of the 3-mile limit, it was true when the 12-mile limit was proclaimed, and it is frighteningly truer still when a 200-mile limit is in prospect. It might be interesting for the government to get some notion of the growth of Canada's responsibilities under these three limits. It is probably known in absolute terms; in fact, I produced such figures during an earlier debate in the House. But the growth rate has never been matched by an enforcement rate. Moving from the 3-mile limit to the 12-mile limit more or less quadrupled the areas over which we assumed jurisdiction and responsibility for control. The step from 12 miles to 200 miles increases the

area by 16 times. Is there any matching 16 times the enforcement capability? None that I can see.
These are substantial increases if looked upon by other comparative means, that is to say, in comparison to our present territorial land mass, where Canada's writ runs. We would be increasing our area of responsibility in the following way: on the Atlantic coast, out 200 miles, we would be increasing it by 15 per cent of our present land mass; on the Pacific coast by 4 per cent, and in the Arctic by 13 per cent; in all, by a total of 32 per cent-these figures are approximate to within a decimal point or so- or one-third more than our present land mass over which we are expected to exercise jurisdiction.
Also, it must be effective jurisdiction. We cannot rely on documents to enforce the law; they do not enforce it on land and they certainly will not do so at sea. If we go beyond 200 miles to the edge of the continental shelf on the east coast, the ultimate claim we are making, we will be adding another 9 per cent to our land mass in jurisdiction; in the Arctic another 3 per cent. In all, these extensions of the area over which Canada is seeking jurisdiction would amount to 45 per cent of our present land mass. Yet we are doing nothing, as far as I can see, to match that increase with enforcement machinery.
We have been told by government spokesmen that there is really no need to worry about policing the seas; that once a convention has been concluded and ratified it will be self-policing. This, of course, is utter nonsense. Canada will have 16 times as much space to play in, but so, of course, will the poachers. They will be able to nip in, say, to 190 miles, conscious that we have nothing afloat which is not of a purely military character which could sail 190 miles out from our shore in time to apprehend poachers.
What do we find in terms of matching this extension in our area of responsibility with enforcement capability? I have heard there are to be three patrol vessels built for the fisheries. They may even be on the stocks already. But we have failed to take the steps required to endow our military forces with the power they need to carry out this enforcement task as a matter of course. I am not speaking of special patrols. When these vessels are on patrol they should be able to act quickly to carry out a fisheries or a pollution control operation at the behest, maybe, of Tele-sat or one of the Argus flights which has detected something and alerted a nearby naval vessel.
As far as I can discern, the government has taken no steps whatever to confer upon our naval commanders a task of this sort, though they are anxious to undertake duties of this kind, tasks which would be meaningful in Canadian terms-and what task could be more meaningful in Canadian terms that the protection of the claim we have made over extended jurisdiction? Nothing has been done to give our naval commanders the authority they need for all time, not just on specific occasions.
There will always be those who are ready to fish closer to land or take a species which is forbidden, as long as nobody is watching. Unfortunately, this is the nature of man, and let us not forget that fishermen are very human and that the fishermen from other nations are perhaps just a little more human in this respect than we would like them to be. We need ocean going vessels capable of highspeed interception at long range with crews not only
June 19, 1975

always at the ready but fully trained in all aspects of their assignment and legally furnished with powers of search and arrest. This is a tall order, but I see no real signs that the government is even gearing up to meet these new and widely enlarged responsibilities in research and in antipollution activity as well as fisheries. I may say I find it incredible that the government should not respond more emphatically to the requirements of the fishermen. This is an important industry on both coasts and, in light of the world food shortage, it is of ever increasing importance. That is why we have brought forward this motion today.
My comments so far have been of a general nature. To set matters in their proper perspective, let me say that on the west coast there are four or five important and apparently unrelated matters which, looked at properly and together, have a direct effect on the size of the salmon catch and what Canada's share of it should be. Some of these matters are technical and unchanging; others are of human creation and therefore changeable, or at least subject to human considerations and capable of being accommodated to the human will.
Mr. Speaker, I have the impression I shall not be able to get to the end of my seven or eight considerations. I will therefore reserve them for another occasion.

"We may differ on the message which results from our reasonings, but not on the goals; they are always the same."

In case the translator did not get that right away, let me say that we differ in method but I do not believe we really differ as to what I am sure our goal must be, which is Canada's jurisdiction over the living resources off our coasts. It is to this end that we are bending so much effort.
I want to thank the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) for recognizing the efforts of our delegation, and who has spoken so generously. Perhaps he, more than anybody else, can understand the sacrifice required of those officials who are away from home for many weeks many times during the year, and who work as hard on the cocktail circuit as they do when writing their briefs, because to them every minute is a moment of work. So once again I thank the hon. member.

speechtext:
I wish to disagree with some hon. members who have said that the wealth of the fisheries is important on the east coast, or important on the west coast. The fisheries are important for Canada as a whole nation. I feel completely free to say that my cabinet colleagues who do not have fisheries in their own responsibilities or ridings recognize that it is important not only to the fishermen but it is part of the wealth not only of this country but also of the world when we think about the protein source that it involves. In fact, it is in recognition of this importance that we came to the rescue of the fisheries last fall and again this spring, and we are now putting together longer term solutions through a reorganization of the fishery which I will be presenting soon to my colleagues.
It is an easy-I was going to say demagogic but I will not; it is an easy temptation to make the fishermen of this country believe that all their problems would go away if only we had unilaterally or multilaterally-attained jurisdiction. The problems would not all go away. We have had crises in the fishing fisheries cyclically over the years which had very little to do with the fact that foreign fleets have been off our shores. I agree that part of our real problem now is due to excessive foreign fishing, and this is one of the reasons we have taken a hard line at ICNAF and elsewhere. But it would be very naive to make our fishermen believe that we did not make some mistakes ourselves in the areas that we manage. I am thinking of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, among other areas, where the pressure is not from international fleets but in many cases from a lack of discipline in managing our own affairs.
Let me comment on some of the things said by the hon. member for St. John's West. The figures he used for 1974 suffered from one distortion; he forgot to say there was a strike in Newfoundland. The present figures show also that there was a strike in Newfoundland in 1975. But despite this, I agree there has been excessive overfishing. As for the comment by Mr. Martin, I am sure he is a responsible man but he must have been misinformed by the press report, because we were saving not only the polar bear but the Arctic which is environmentally the most fragile part of our country.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich waxed considerably indignant and I say this with all the respect and affection that I have for him, when he discovered that my

June 19, 1975
National Resources
colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) had caught in. his net something that the opposition obviously did not expect, namely, a fault in the motion. But it is to this motion that we must address ourselves, and to the amendment brought in, in good grace and good haste.
Extraordinary opposition solidarity was displayed by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). I must say that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich showed such great support and solidarity that any idea I had that there were rifts in the Conservative caucus have gone out of the window. Because if he were able to second that motion and to support it when he saw the flaw that it contained, I must say I am very much impressed by his sense of solidarity.
When he says to us that we are being political, I would invite him to read more carefully the speech of the hon. member for St. John's West. He obviously read the motion before it was given to us yesterday morning, and if he is appealing to us to take an all-party position, then surely the least we should have had was a copy of that motion for a little longer than 24 or 36 hours. Surely there could have been an approach to bring about unanimity in the House, a suggestion asking us to support strongly the efforts of our delegation and of the government and many members of the opposition who were valued and useful advisers to our delegations in Geneva and Caracas.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
If the hon. member for St. John's West had wanted to have unanimity, surely he would have consulted us. I might have been able to support a motion drafted by the hon. member for St. John's West because, as I have said, I too want Canada to have exclusive management rights over the living resources off our coasts. I might say the hon. member has not even approached me yet to sign his famous petition with which he is going from village to village in Newfoundland. I hope that in his pilgrimage he is also taking the time to learn of some of the things we are doing in Newfoundland to improve the quality of the fish through our incentive program of 2lA cents for first-quality fish. I have been informed by my inspection branch that this is bringing about a minor miracle. Never before has such good quality fish been delivered to the plants. I hope the hon. member for St. John's West has time to look at this situation. These are some of the positive steps we have taken to benefit the fishery.
I want to apologize on behalf of my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs; he could not be present during this debate since he has left for Japan. I also want to thank the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for his support, especially his suggestion regarding the consumption of fish across Canada. Fish is good for our health, and when I grew up we were told that it was good for our brains. The House could pass a unanimous resolution if it wanted to do something useful for the fishermen, possibly to return to the meatless Friday.
May I say a few words about the speech of the hon. member for New Westminster. He talked about daffodils. I want to tell him the daffodils are good and strong, and that the salmon enhancement program will go ahead. We

have the active and good co-operation of the government of British Columbia, which is working with us in identifying the best streams-and I want to say that publicly. However, I find it difficult to agree completely with the hon. member for New Westminster when he tells me that unilateralism would protect the salmon on the west coast.
I wonder what plebiscite there has been among the fishermen in the hon. member's native province, because I happen to have been there recently and I know some of them are very worried and concerned. It has been a very difficult task to have salmon referred to in the unified text we now have. This has been the result of extraordinary efforts on the part of our delegation and everyone concerned. To give that away lightly, until I have other evidence, and until we have talked to those nations which are putting pressure upon our salmon stocks on the high seas, would appear to me to be the height of irresponsibility.
I would agree with the goals, the aims, and the objectives of the hon. member for St. John's West. In other words, I assume that his objectives are not merely political, but rather are directed at the protection of Canadian fisheries and the whole range of industries dependent on the fisheries. Unfortunately the phrasing of his motion makes it very difficult for me to support, and obviously would achieve little, if anything. It would be of no help to Canadian fisheries or Canadian fishermen, or to Canada's fisheries negotiators. I am not sure it would be of much help to the opposition, but I am not responsible for their concern. My concern as the Minister of State (Fisheries) is to go beyond meaningless statements of generalities. I have said before that fish stocks cannot be rebuilt on negotiating texts, and they cannot be rebuilt on motions either.
The motion before us is unrealistic and ill-considered because it does not take into account both state practice and the emerging consensus at the Law of the Sea Conference which indicates overwhelming support for the 200-mile limit for the exclusive fisheries rights of the coastal state. It has not been easy to bring about the recognition of the 200-mile limit, a recognition which is on the verge of being formalized in international law.
It would be unwise to go against our own achievement, as suggested in the motion of the hon. member. It would also be unwise simply to ignore the international legitimacy that now attaches to the 200-mile limit. It would be unwise for Canada to isolate itself even from other coastal states and assert a unilateral claim over the whole of the fisheries resources of the continental shelf and beyond 200 miles. To do so would be to fly in the face of our supporters and opponents alike. Any action we take to protect Canadian fisheries must be effective action. Even unilateral action does not mean acting against the views of the majority of states and attempting to impose the views of one country upon all countries. Unilateral action of this kind has never been successful.
The motion proposed by the hon. member for St. John's West is also unrealistic in that it ignores what the government has already done and is doing for Canadian fisheries. Indeed it suggests we have done nothing, and hence
June 19, 1975

should begin to act immediately. Let me say that immediately is not soon enough. If we had waited until the present time to act we would have been quite irresponsible. That is why we began years ago. Following the failure of the 1958 and 1960 Conferences on the Law of the Sea to resolve the problem of fisheries jurisdiction, the government unilaterally extended Canada's fishing limit to 12 miles. That was done in 1970, and not in the period from 1957 to 1962 when the party opposite sat on the treasury benches.
Today that does not seem like a great accomplishment. At the time, however, the fishing industry attached great importance to the 12-mile limit, and it was internationally controversial. We acted to implement it after having exhausted all possibilities of agreement, and soon we found that even countries which had opposed us were doing the same thing.
Subsequently, in 1970, my predecessor went still further and closed the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the Bay of Fundy, Queen Charlotte Sound, Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait as exclusive Canadian fishing zones. We negotiated phasing-out agreements with the countries concerned, and as a result important foreign operations off our coasts are already coming to an end. This was effective action covering an area as great as would be a 200-mile limit for many countries. At the same time, however, this did not lead to a cod war or to a challenge before the International Court of Justice, as did Iceland's latest efforts to extend its fisheries jurisdiction unilaterally.
We have not taken a back seat to anyone, and I do not believe we need take lessons from anyone in this field. We have been leaders, not followers, and the reason we have succeeded is that we have always gone that extra mile, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich understands so well. We have gone that extra mile toward obtaining international agreement before striking out on our own. We have always taken into account not only our own interests but those of other countries. We have not done this because we are boy scouts but because we are realists, and because we wanted to succeed, and we did succeed.
In more recent years Canada has continued to be among the leaders of those countries pressing for a still further extension of fisheries jurisdiction at the Law of the Sea Conference. We have already gained overwhelming recognition for the concept of the 200-mile limit. It is only a matter of time before this concept becomes incorporated in international law.
However, we do not believe there is time to wait for the concept to be incorporated in treaty law before acting upon it. At this very moment the Canadian delegation at ICNAF is pressing for a reduction of foreign fishing fleet effort by some 40 per cent, for lower total allowable catches of stocks whose levels of abundance have very seriously declined, and for a 100 per cent preference for Canadian fishermen in the harvest of certain stocks of particular importance to us.
These proposals in fact anticipate the results of the Law of the Sea Conference. They are an immediate assertion of Canada's right to manage and control its coastal fisheries resources. If the other member states of ICNAF are not completely blind to reality, then our proposals will be accepted. On the other hand, if certain members of ICNAF
National Resources
refuse to co-operate with Canada in the orderly development of a new coastal fisheries regime, then Canada will be obliged to consider other means of protecting its legitimate interests.
I am well aware of the fishing industry's views on the past performance of ICNAF. Nevertheless, Canada's accomplishments within ICNAF should not be under rated. Only four short years ago the foreign fleets off our east coast operated with virtually no restrictions. At that time Canada had no capability for effective surveillance of foreign fishing activity. Now virtually every stock of commercial importance-almost 60 in all-is under quota control, and Canadian shares of such quotas have steadily increased. These are the concrete, practical results achieved by the government.
Furthermore, in 1974 a start was made to reduce quotas below estimated maximum sustained yield levels, and Canadian patrol vessels conducted almost 300 boardings of foreign fishing craft. These operations have put the foreign fleets on their mettle, and in a number of cases have resulted in improved adherence to agreed ICNAF regulations.
Unfortunately our increased surveillance has also established beyond doubt that certain countries are violating these agreed regulations with complete disregard for their international treaty obligations. We are not going to tolerate such behaviour. We will use every means available to put a stop to it. The distant-water fishing countries cannot argue on the one hand that fisheries management must be based on international agreements and, on the other hand, act contrary to such agreements.

speechtext:
If we are to secure an effective and comprehensive protection for the broad range of interests of Canadian fisheries, we have to take into account the fact that a simple, unilateral extension of jurisdiction will not protect our $100 million west coast salmon fisheries and our threatened Atlantic salmon fisheries. We must continue our efforts to reach international agreement on fisheries problems at the Law of the Sea Conference, in ICNAF and other international fisheries commissions, and through bilateral negotiations and such discussions as those I had yesterday with the minister of fisheries from Norway. These efforts are not incompatible with other forms of action that may prove necessary.
There is a limit not only to our patience but to the ability of the stocks and of our fishing industry to survive under present conditions. Unilateral action is one of the options open to us. Even unilateral action, however, requires negotiations if it is to be effective and successful, as it was when Canada moved unilaterally in 1964 and 1970.
I believe that in all public discussions of this question, especially with groups of fishermen, there is a responsibility to tell them that even if we were given jurisdiction tomorrow morning, and even if we declared unilateral jurisdiction, foreign fleets would not all disappear as if by magic. That is misleading and it is demagoguery.
We cannot guarantee instant results no matter what course we take, but I am confident that we can bring about timely results. No government has done more than ours in the way of both national and international action for the protection of coastal fisheries and coastal fishermen. We know that the future of our coastal communities is linked with our fisheries. We shall not only protect that future but make it better than ever. Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the House for its patience and tolerance.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate today in this debate on fisheries and on problems that relate directly and indirectly to the fishing industry. This also gives me an opportunity to endorse the unanimous request of the provincial legislature in my own province of Nova Scotia that the federal government unilaterally declare jurisdiction over the 200 mile fishing zone along the coast.
During the recent Law of the Sea Conference in Geneva I was privileged to serve for a few weeks as an adviser to the Canadian delegation. I found this to be a very stimulating and informative experience. This particular conference was the biggest in the history of the world. Some 146 delegations participated at the conference, and from personal discussions I held with the deputy ministers of fisheries for the U.S.S.R., Norway, and Denmark I found that the conference was regarded as the most important gathering since the San Francisco Conference at which the UN charter was drafted.
Basically the conference attempted to develop a constitution which would be accepted by all states as a binding treaty obligation. It went far beyond merely codifying existing concepts. What the conference tried to do was to alter radically the traditional or classical legal concepts on
[Mr. LeBlanc (Westmorland-Kent).)
which the Law of the Sea had been founded for the past 300 years.
The subject matter of the conference was very wide ranging, and the issues were incredibly complex. They involved highly sensitive military questions, extremely important economic considerations, as well as far reaching social implications flowing from some of the new concepts being developed. Oil alone, for example, and the search for it, illustrates the importance we attach to two questions. One is the breadth of the continental shelf over which a coastal state would have sovereign rights for the purpose of exploration and exploitation of the resources, and the second is the delimitation of the area of the sea bed beyond national jurisdiction to be reserved for purely peaceful purposes, as well as for the common heritage of mankind. I point out these two items as being very important.
The legal regime, and the international machinery that will need to be established for the rational management of future resources, could affect the thinking of peoples and of governments on the whole problem of the rational utilization of increasingly scarce international resources.
The pre-existing Law of the Sea, and indeed the whole of the international law, has been based on two simple principles, one being the sovereignty of states, and the other, freedom on the high seas.
The economic zone, or the 200 mile concept as recently proposed, is a radical new approach which permits some elements of the regime of the high seas, such as freedom of navigation, but partakes also of some of the rights included in the concept of sovereignty. In my opinion, this is a matter of some regret.
As the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) stated when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on May 26:
The Geneva session of the Law of the Sea Conference did not, unfortunately, give us the new international convention that Canada, and Canadian fishermen especially, have been seeking for many years ... Perhaps the most significant development at the Geneva session was the emergence of a single negotiating text on which the conference can base its work at the next session to be held early in 1976. This text in no way represents an agreement. It does, however, provide the conference with a valuable aid to negotiation that should facilitate its progress.
This is simply not good enough. Mr. Speaker, may we adjourn to go to the other place?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just before the House rose at six o'clock I had begun my speech. I had placed on record something the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) said when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on May 26. He said, in part:
National Resources
Perhaps the most significant development at the Geneva session was the emergence of a single negotiating text on which the conference can base its work at the next session to be held early in 1976. This text in no way represents an agreement. It does, however, provide the conference with a valuable aid to negotiation that should facilitate its progress.
In my view, Madam Speaker, this is simply not good enough. Our fishermen and all those connected with the industry have heard this excuse, this old record played ever since 1958. "Don't despair" says the minister; "Hang in there; wait until we have another conference. Maybe, just maybe, we can get some of these problems resolved next year, at the next conference, or two, or maybe three." In the meantime every foreign nation under the sun appears to be taking advantage of our fisheries resources and raping, pillaging, and plundering our stocks, until many of our species are now below what is called the sustainable yield level.
In my opinion the Minister of Fisheries, the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) must share the blame equally for the fact that the Geneva conference did not produce any written agreement or definite solutions to the many problems facing the Canadian fishing industry. I say this not out of disrespect for the hard working team from the Department of External Affairs which presented Canada's position at the conference, under the capable direction of our ambassador to Austria, Mr. A. Beesley. From my observations, those people were aggressive and diligent in the performance of their duties. But I point out that they all work at the civil service level, and decisions were to be made at the conference at the political level. Other nations, especially Russia, which has the largest fishing fleet operating on our continental shelf, recognized this fact. They sent their top civil servants and top political representatives to the conference, where they stayed from the beginning to the end.
There is absolutely no reason why at least one of the three ministers I mentioned could not have been at the Law of the Sea conference from the day it started until it closed. Their presence would have served to notify all the nations of the world that Canada, when presenting its position, was making a serious and determined attempt to establish the point that we believe that the coastal state must have exclusive management of offshore resources, at least out to the 200-mile limit. It must have the right to set the allowable catch, and the right to reserve to itself as much of that catch as it has the capacity to take.
Instead of attending constantly at the most important conference held since the beginning of mankind-I actually believe that, because since the beginning of history nations have fought to control the sea and the conference had to do with who would control over two thirds of the world's surface-the ministers condescended to drop in from time to time, when it was convenient to them. This laissez-faire attitude cost our fishermen and nation dearly in lost prestige and in lack of agreement on many controversial points.
The attitude of some delegates was, "Surely Canada is not serious in its presentation, not serious in its claims to all the continental shelf off its shores, because there are no cabinet ministers at the conference to back up her claims." Madam Speaker, if the government was sincere in its
29576-26/4

June 19, 1975
National Resources
efforts on behalf of our fishermen, one or more of the three cabinet ministers I mentioned would have attended at Geneva at all times, to persuade, to argue, to convince, to reason and, if necessary, to fight for the rights of our fishermen.
I say this because of what we have at stake. We have the second largest coastline in the world, washed by three oceans, the Atlantic, the Arctic, and the Pacific. Our country has a direct interest in the wise management of the seas. As one of the world's principal coastal states we have a particular interest in that 20 per cent ribbon of the total sea area which extends over our continental shelf and margin. As a coastal state we should have special opportunities as well as special obligations. We have more to lose than any other country in the world if, for example, our marine environment is contaminated by pollution or if our living resources are depleted by over fishing.
We do not seek these rights purely out of self-interest. As Canadians, we want the world's shipping to move as freely as possible, not only into and out of Canadian ports but everywhere on the world's oceans. However, we are very concerned about the biological consequences of pollution and about over fishing, matters which, as things stand today, are beyond the control of the coastal state. These are matters which should be of concern not only to coastal states and to Canada; they should concern all nations.
I happen to be one of those who believe that through wise management of our nearby waters we can protect a vital world interest. We can protect the world's peoples from the dire consequences which are bound to ensue if we continue on our present course and if we fail to treat the world's seas as an area to be managed and protected. The concept of the freedom of the high seas has been abused by all nations, to the point that it has become a freedom to over fish and a licence to pollute. It has served the interests of the few, under the guise of a principle which purports to protect the interests of everyone. In my opinion the coastal state must be given the power to protect its interest on those questions.
When making these claims Canadians at times are accused of being very acquisitive. However, may I point out that if our approach were adopted, all the new coastal rights would be paralleled by the acceptance of new duties and obligations.
Moreover, if there is concern about peoples of the world benefiting from the concepts I am proposing, I would point out that the vast majority of the world's people, well over 90 per cent, reside in the coastal states. Coastal states form the largest part of the international community. It is the coastal states which will undoubtedly benefit from the wise management of our marine resources.
Our efforts today should be both environmental and economic. We must know exactly how far our continental shelf or margin extends seaward. We must pay more attention to where the fish stocks are, and where they spend most of their natural lives. We have not done this in the past, which accounts for the failure of the International Commission for the North Atlantic Fisheries to protect our own Canadian interest.

We have drawn grids and numbered them one, two, three, four, five and six, and 1A, 2G, 3P, 4V, 5Z and 6C, without first consulting the fishermen or the fish. Now, the fish are not aware of our artificial lines and the fish know no international boundaries. However, our fishermen, especially along the south shore of Nova Scotia, are well aware of the government's grid system. While countries signatory to the ICNAF arrangements have fished on our continental shelf, our own fishermen have been fined and forced, not into a bootlegging as they did many years ago, but into what I call a "fishlegging" operation, in order to earn sufficient money to provide for their families and pay off their loans annually to the provincial loan board, their first and primary obligation.
I would be the first to agree that we should be concerned about conservation and the wise management of all our precious marine resources. However, I say to the government and the minister that charity begins at home, a point the minister would do well to take into consideration. It is unfair and unjust to apply strictly the conservation rules and regulations to Canadian fisherman when you do not have the power to enforce the same rules upon the nationals of other countries who are destroying our fish stocks. This is the kind of thing for which the minister and the government are responsible.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
According to the reports of our surveillance officials, the number of fishing vessels in the ICNAF areas off the east coast ranged from a high of 1,000 to a low of 300 in the month of December. Of this fleet, 502 belonged to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, 100 belonged to Poland and the balance was split up among Canada and other ICNAF fishing countries. Obviously we are being over run and over fished on our own doorstep.
I recognize that the most satisfactory way to arrive at international law is by negotiation and agreement among nations, but it is not the only way. We can take unilateral action to extend our area of fisheries jurisdiction to the continental margin or 200 miles, whichever is farthest, pending the final outcome of the next Law of the Sea Conference. If the conference accepts our stand, there will be no problem. If it does not, we will have indicated to the world that, in Canada's view, the sovereign rights of coastal states, as defined under the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf and confirmed by the International Court of Justice, already extend and should be maintained out to the limits of the continental margin.
This action would not only ensure protection for our fisheries resources, but it would also ensure Canadian ownership for the oil, gas, and mineral resources on our continental shelf. It would also ensure Canadian regulation of all scientific research in this area. It is up to us as Canadians, and it is up to the government to give leadership on this issue.
Time is of the essence if we are to save the fish processing industry and the fish stocks upon which the industry and our coastal communities depend from total and irreparable hardship. Let's face it, unless we take action to conserve our marine resources there will be no fish for anyone, and when there are no fish there is nothing to negotiate.
June 19, 1975

Sometimes it is said we are all the same. However, I think maritimers are a little different. We have a kinship with the west. We like to look at the wide open spaces.

speechtext: And a kinship with New Brunswick.

speechtext:
Yes, we have a kinship with New Brunswick because it is a maritime province as well. I suppose you need to be a maritimer to really understand the vicious circumstances presently plaguing the fishing industry. We have declining catches of practically all species, and rising industry costs on everything required by the industry from paint to rope to maintenance and fuel oil. We have poor markets and prices which cost the established companies millions of dollars last year. This threatened the jobs of 35,000 fishermen as well as the jobs of thousands of plant workers and their dependents who live in the region.
In order to stave off immediate disaster the federal government gave the industry two financial transfusions recently, bringing the total aid since last fall to something like $85 million. This band-aid has been helpful, but I say to the minister in all seriousness that it is no solution to our long-term problems and it has been inadequate to cover the real need. In fact the aid provided compares almost exactly to the increase in collecting our income taxes by the Department of National Revenue from 1974 to 1975.
I have tried to rationalize why the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) went to the Law of the Sea Conference. The only rationalization I can see is that the cost of collecting our taxes reached the same amount that was provided to Atlantic Canada in the past few months. It was the least amount the government could give considering the population in the four Atlantic provinces; Newfoundland, 546,000; Prince Edward Island, 118,000; Nova Scotia, 818,000; New Brunswick, 670,000. There are 2,152,000 people in that area of Canada, all of whom are dependent, either entirely or in part, on this important fishing industry. These are facts I would like the minister to consider when talking about the aid being provided to our area.
In closing I would ask the minister, when convenient, to tell this House where some of the money is going. What consultants have been hired by the Fisheries and Marine Service of the Department of the Environment in the last two years? It would certainly be of interest to this House if we knew their names, qualifications, salaries, duties, the length of their employment, and whether tenders were called for these positions before they were hired or whether they were appointed for some other reason. This is important because the fishermen, certainly those in my constituency, are starting to question the regulations and the various moves being made by the department which have a serious effect upon their livelihood. In their opinion we can drift along with a few landlubbers on the payroll, but it would appear that our fisheries department is starting to flounder and sink from the wrong advice from the wrong people in the wrong place at the wrong time. This was obvious when fishermen from Atlantic Canada appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and gave their views on subsidy regulations, fishing licences, the construction of slipways and docks, and export regulations.
National Resources
It is also my understanding that the minister began reorganizing his department some nine months ago. Since that time all we have heard are rumours concerning this reorganization. One rumour is that the industrial development branch will be established outside Ottawa. Another is that certain changes are to be made in senior advisory personnel. What are the changes to be made? The rumours are not surprising in light of the statement made by the Minister of the Environment at the inauguration of the Captain Bernier Laboratories at Longueuil on May 28, 1975, when she said, and I quote:
Precise instructions have been given so that Environment Canada will favour the participation of French-speaking candidates in terms both of quality and number in all relevant competitions aimed at filling positions at the middle and upper management levels in the scientific, professional and technical fields.
Whatever happened to the bilingual regulations as laid down by the government? Does this new regulation mean that if employees are required by the minister's department in the scientific, professional, and technical fields they will not be acceptable if they are unilingual English even if they are willing to take French lessons in order to qualify? If this is so, it may well be possible that a highly qualified English-speaking scientist whose services might be invaluable to Canada and the fishing industry would be ignored by the government simply because he did not speak both languages when applying for employment.
