speechtext:
-and with good reason if he found those things irrelevant to the people of his constituency.
I am sure hon. members who have already taken part in this debate will agree that this is not simply a debate about fisheries. It is about food for mankind, about conservation of the world's resources and the most efficient use we can make of those limited resources for the benefit of humanity. So I rise, not to speak for the fishermen of York-Scarborough but perhaps, if Your Honour will permit the expression, to spread the net wider in this debate and put it into what I believe should be the context of every debate in this House for some time to come, that is to say, a global context.
We have heard a good deal today about the needs of our fishermen and of our economy. There have been a few references to the importance of Canadian policy in this respect in terms of its effect upon the world community. But there has not been sufficient attention to that aspect of the matter, in my opinion.
At a time when roughly half the world is verging on starvation, when there are some 200 million under-nourished children, when some 10 million people, most of them children, will probably die during this year from starvation related illnesses, I think we are obliged to talk about this subject under discussion today in terms that are wider than merely our own benefit and self interest.
I, like other members on this side who have spoken, share the objectives of the mover and seconder of this resolution. Certainly I share the objectives of our negotiators who have worked so hard over many years to provide
June 19, 1975

leadership in the world, in terms of developing a regime of law and progressive management of our resources of the sea. But I differ from the mover of the resolution and the mover of the amendment because I think they are taking a bigger grasp on behalf of Canada than perhaps we can justify.
I note that speakers in favour of the resolution and the amendment are recommending that we claim the greater of the 200 mile zone and the continental shelf. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) pointed out that as far as the east coast is concerned this might involve at least 400 miles. I ask my hon. friends who are proposing a claim of this magnitude whether or not they think it is reasonable, whether or not they think it can be sustained in the international forums where we must argue our case?
We must be careful, Madam Speaker, not to appear, as I believe we have already been accused of appearing, to be engaged in the great sea grab of the twentieth century, a sea grab which might challenge in scope and magnitude the land grabs of the nineteenth century. I hope we will not earn the reputation of being the imperialists of the sea, that we will not appear to the majority of the world less well endowed than we to be demanding too great a share of the world's resources.
Already we must be conscious of the fact that we have more than our share in terms of our population. We are rich beyond imagination compared to most of the people in the world. When I hear that we are asserting jurisdiction over an area equal to something like 45 per cent of our land mass, although this additional territory might be very attractive to us as Canadians, I wonder whether we can justify to the world what surely must seem to be greed, when we have so much and lay claim to so much more.
I say this having full regard to the situation of our coastal peoples, particularly our fishermen and those who depend on them. I think we should negotiate vigorously on their behalf. We certainly do not want their interests to be prejudiced unfairly from any foreign source, but I think our main interest and theirs surely must be as trustees for the resources over which we have control-trustees for all of humanity.
Although we should ensure, as managers of our sovereign territory, that our own people have a fair share of those resources, our prime responsibility must be to work for the rational management of the world's resources. We happen by good fortune to have access to a great many of those resources. According to existing international law we have control over many of them. In development of the Law of the Sea we have brought the world community to a position where we will probably have an acknowledged power of decision over a great deal more territory than that over which we have hitherto exercised control.
I appeal to the members of this House to think of this policy that we are developing on resources of the sea in terms of the global responsibility that we have. Hon. members must be more aware than most of our fellow citizens how the age of plenty and of waste in the world is already past, and how we have now entered the age of scarcity, an age that demands conservation, and sane and rational management of resources.
National Resources
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has put the challenge as the challenge of sharing. Let us look at this subject as part of the challenge to the world of surviving on this planet together, of sharing its resources wisely, of attaining by co-operation among peoples a more just distribution of the world's wealth-a global just society, if you like, just as we are trying to create a just society within our own nation.
The most recent report of the Club of Rome, the second report, "Mankind at the Turning Point", makes it clear that the only way we are going to be successful in tackling the interlocking challenges of population, food, energy, and materials-these pervasive crises that all of us in the world today share-is through global planning and cooperation. That is why I am reluctant to accept the approach inherent in this resolution today. This approach is one which implies that co-operation seems impossible, that we must give up hope of international agreement for rational and co-operative effort on the part of nations of the world to achieve the objectives on which we all agree.
I do not share that pessimism. I do not share that negative approach to international co-operation. Our negotiators at the Conference on the Law of the Sea have achieved great progress, and if we can continue to work with as much conviction, as much dedication, and as much imagination as we have I think we will be able to convince the world of the need to conserve our resources in the way we see as being in our interests as well as the interests of all mankind.
At this point I should like to say a few words about international co-operation because the attitude expressed in this resolution is perhaps symptomatic of a general distrust and disillusionment with government, not only national but international. Just as we as parliamentarians have a responsibility to restore the faith of our constituents in this institution of parliament, we have a responsibility to restore the faith of the people of the world in co-operative international institutions to which we belong, and in which we have put our faith for the solution of world problems in substitution for the old method of war.
It should be stressed that if we are to solve problems through co-operation we must have institutions like the United Nations in which we can pursue those solutions. The United Nations is under attack because so many of us are unhappy about the way in which it has carried on its work, particularly in the last year. I had the privilege of being a Canadian delegate to the United Nations General Assembly last fall, and I shared these frustrations that so many Canadians and others felt about the way the United Nations seemed to be going.
However, we have nothing else as promising as the United Nations to use as a vehicle for this co-operation which is more than ever necessary among the peoples of the world. We should recognize that through the United Nations we have focused the attention of the nations of the world, in a way which we otherwise could not have done, on the problems of population, food, environment, and the sea, and we have made progress. We have made progress that should encourage us that the crises that afflict the world can be attacked through co-operative

June 19, 1975
National Resources
effort, and we should devote increasing effort to achieve co-operative solutions rather than throw up our hands in desperation, relying on unilateral action such as is recommended in this resolution.
Unilateral action, as has been said here today, should be a last resort. It may be a necessary resort. If we do end by relying on unilateral action I hope it will be because we see it being necessary not only in our self-interest but also in the interests of mankind.
I urge that we continue to work, as we have worked at the Law of the Sea Conference, with our global responsibilities in the forefront of our minds. If we do that I think we will also do justice to our own fishermen and our own people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY OVER LIVING RESOURCES OF CONTINENTAL SHELF AND SLOPE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate and I want at the outset to commend my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter), whose motion could not be more timely. I hope I can add a few comments in support of the very excellent approach he has taken in pleading that Canada, through this parliament, should immediately assert its right over the continental shelf and slopes, and thereby save the dying fishing industry before it is too late.
Certainly the motion should commend itself to all members on both sides of this House, because surely it is long past the time when Canada must show some backbone and assure protection of its marine resources with some positive action, instead of by diplomatic message and through idle threats made in speeches that have been taking place over the past decade.
I find it very strange that everyone in Canada at every level of interest, including the provincial governments in those regions that depend on the fishing industry at least in part for their economy, should support the suggestion that Canada should assert itself and take unilateral action, with the exception of the government opposite.
Every last fisherman in this country who depends on representation in this House by members of parliament on both sides wants Canada to take the action necessary to protect the industry which has and can continue to be the means of his livelihood, and wants Canada to assert its rights over our God given resources.
I would venture to say that certainly every member who represents a district with any fisheries prominence would want the government to take immediate action to declare our rights, and will want to vote for this motion. I would even venture to say that the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) would like to support our motion, and hopefully he will along with his colleagues. Unfortunately he is guided by the few wise men of the inner circle, those few wise men who would not know a fish from a piece of tainted meat, and could not care less about what happens to our fishing industry.
Unfortunately the minister is beginning to have the same trouble with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) that the previous minister, Mr. Davies, had with the then Secretary of State for External Affairs. I must say that the present minister deserves every commendation for the manner in which he has tackled his new responsibilities since taking office, and I

respect his sincerity and his attitude, just as I did his predecessor, but I fear he is falling into the same trap with his senior colleagues.
The minister does not know who are his real friends. I would remind him that every member of this House concerned with fisheries is his friend, regardless of which side he sits on. I think this has been reflected in the attitude shown the minister since the session started. He should pay a little more attention to their advice instead of too much attention to the Lucases, the Doucets and the Nee-dlers who continue to guide the fortunes of the fisheries department by remote control, by scientific studies, by charts, and by sitting around in their board rooms making decisions which are meaningless.
The minister has already made thousands of friends among the fishermen in Canada because of his evident sincerity in trying to revitalize the industry, but unless he can convince his colleagues in the cabinet that that is really needed, and unless they can show some guts and take the necessary action, I am afraid the minister will have nothing left to revitalize.
If my figures are correct, we have spent some $80 million in subsidies to fishermen this year alone. Finally we are recognizing the need for making the hundreds of fishing communities more self-sufficient by providing more funds for small craft harbours and more business by supporting quality control in cooling and chilling facilities, by providing boat building assistance, and by initiating licensing programs. But if we do not show some backbone we will have nothing left to control or to cool, because it is obvious that the stocks will be depleted to oblivion.
How much longer will the fishermen in the Atlantic region, where the industry is so vital to the economy, listen to meaningless announcements of the action Canada may take or expects to take at the Law of the Sea conferences or at ICNAF meetings? How much longer are the fishermen of Newfoundland going to wait? They are getting sick and tired of hearing what Canada may do or expects to do. How much longer will they rely on the vague promises that Canada expects full acceptance of its proposals for the 1976 season calling for a 40 per cent reduction in the foreign fishing effort and increased allocations for Canada?
Then we hear the minister say that the meetings are purely scientific and that no one with authority attends them but the scientists. Are the fishermen going to believe his words when he threatens the refusal of our eastern ports to foreign draggers? His predecessor used the same words back in 1973, and the action he took was to commission a study to determine the effects on eastern ports in case we refuse the use of these ports. Where is the study? Probably gathering dust, as are all the rest of the studies.
Fisheries in Newfoundland are the mainstay of that province's economy. Fishermen are trying to exist peacefully, but I cannot assure the minister as to how much longer they will remain peaceful if the government continues to act by diplomatic message and to protest with meaningless words.
June 19, 1975

What will happen, even if we do get agreement on quotas? What happened as a result of the incident in 1973 when the Soviet Union had taken their quota of herring of 48,200 tons on the Georges Bank by July 20? Yet on September 5, 20, and 25, they were still fishing herring in considerable quantities, but no action was taken because our government considered these to be minor incidents. The government asked for a report, and it was not until September 27 when the details were confirmed that the former minister of fisheries made Moscow aware of what was going on, as if they did not already know. A message was sent to the Soviet Atlantic fleet commander to request that he take immediate action to bring the illegal activities to a halt.
Then what happened? On October 3, almost three months later, another Soviet vessel was boarded and found to have 20 tons of herring. There were five other Soviet vessels fishing herring, but they took off to evade boarding. All this was happening at a time when Canadian fishermen were abiding by the quotas set. I wonder what was the outcome of that incident. I say that those nations will continue to ignore any further quotas on which the government might insist and which might be accepted.
I hope the minister will be able to enforce the new quotas. I did not hear anything inspiring in the interview which took place this morning with Dr. Needier, who is still at the Edinburgh conference. Apparently they are not too successful. I ask, if we do get agreement, will the Soviets and other nations abide by the rules, or will they continue to ignore our 12 miles limit and our inadequate patrol force, and destroy our inshore fishermen's gear while nothing else is done other than to ask for reports from regional directors and send polite notes to embassies?
I can tell the minister that the fishermen will not listen much longer. They are becoming more and more discouraged each day and each season. They are sufficiently discouraged as it is with recurring ice conditions which prevent them from having access to the water, and with waiting for our inadequate ice breaker to open up the avenues they require to the fishing zones or to permit them to carry out inshore fishery. When will Canada finally build another ice breaker? Probably it will be ready in two or three years when the fish are all gone.
I do not think it will be much longer before our fishermen, who must survive, start copying the example set by that small nation, Iceland, which insists on her right to survive by forcing agreement to her 50 mile limit. If no agreement at the Law of the Sea Conference is reached, she will extend her limits farther out.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the problems with which our fishermen are faced now, need not have grown to the present proportions if Canada had realized the potential of our fisheries and the value of our fish stocks many years ago. We have reached a stage now at which we are reacting by ad hoc programs, which would have been unnecessary had we realized the potential of our fisheries, as did the foreign nations. We are being outfished, out manoeuvred, outmarketed, and indeed laughed at by the Russians, the Europeans, the Japanese, and even the South Koreans and others who saw the value of our fisheries and whose aim it is to sell in the global markets. Since the
National Resources
early 1960's they began deploying their new distant-water fleets that have either processing or freezing equipment on board, or else are mothered by big factory ships to enable them to remain at sea for months at a time.
Let me give you an example of how we have fallen behind because of the lack of realization and lack of foresight by the present and past governments regarding the value of our fish stocks. In September of 1973 there was convincing proof that the Norwegians were seriously engaged in catching capelin on the Grand Banks. A 585 foot factory ship had been processing capelin since June of that year. The ship, with a crew of 55, was being supplied by ten smaller ships and was capable of loading the finished product aboard cargo boats at sea for delivery to world markets. Russian factory ships had been fishing for capelin two seasons previously.
What was Canada doing in the meantime? In the same year, fish plant operators were doing a survey of the market potential in Japan. In October of that same year, after the fact, came the big announcement by Canada that as a result of the findings of an exploratory survey costing $1.3 million it was learned that there were abundant stocks of capelin sufficient to support a commercial fishery. At that time the Norwegians and Russians were selling in these markets for a couple of years.
I will never understand why Canada did not know that. All we had to do was to ask the Norwegians about the prospective capelin resource. All we had to do was to send Dr. Needier or Mr. Lucas to Norway, throw a cocktail party for a couple of thousand dollars, and they would have had the answers required, instead of spending over $1 million.
What more glaring example is there to illustrate our neglect of our fisheries resource than the increasing value of that resource as food, not only for our own use in Canada but to fulfill our commitments to assist the starving nations of the world? What better example of its value is there at present when Canadians are so reluctant to buy meat because of the meat scandal?
These facts demand that the highest priority be given to getting the maximum value from what we have left, and to extending our fish resources. Not only is there a need for that resource as an available source of nutrition at a reasonable price to the consumer and an available source of food to feed the starving nations, but also as a source of livelihood for the thousands of fishermen whom we must protect, and for whom we must get the maximum price and security by providing them with adequate facilities and obtaining full value for their labour. We must extend every effort to market the product to the advantage of the fishermen, the processors, and the consumers who are increasingly burdened by inflation. One wonders why the fishermen and consumers at the two opposing ends are being affected the most.
I ask the minister again how the thousands of fishermen in Canada can continue to believe him, when on May 26 he stated to the Standing Committee of Fisheries and Forestry the following:
We hope our appeal for co-operation will be heard in ICNAF. We believe that the progress achieved at the Law of the Sea Conference

June 19, 1975
National Resources
should have laid the foundation for co-operation along these lines. Certainly the outcome of the ICNAF meeting will have to be taken into account in the Canadian government's appraisal of the results of the Law of the Sea Conference, as it will have to be taken into account in the determination of any further action that may be necessary to promote the development of the new international fisheries regime that has already made so much headway in the world.
How can I believe these words, when just three days previously I read that France would demand access to traditional fishing waters, and when I read that the French secretary of state for fisheries said that his government accepts the concept of an economic zone for protection of fish stocks, but that his government will not accept any scheme which would forbid French fishermen from working in the coastal waters of another state?
How can I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Dr. Needier or Mr. Lucas, when in the same article I read that a French expert who specializes in marine affairs said that it is unlikely that the Canadian position would be accepted if it meant that the French fishermen would suffer, and when he went on to say that French fishermen have been operating off the Canadian coast for hundreds of years and feel that they have some priority on the fish according to traditional rights?
They are correct in their assumption that there is no doubt that if the industry is to be saved some controls will have to be imposed, but the French are not likely to respond favourably to any scheme which would wall off their traditional fishing waters. They are right when they say that, rather than restricting the French, other nations should be cut off first. As is further stated, a common position could be arrived at with the French nation because Canada cannot expect to take 100 per cent of the catch, and I am sure that a bilateral agreement could be worked out as to management and control.
What I resent most is that the government opposite thinks Canadians, particularly those directly involved, are naive enough to believe that all is well, that all we need is to show a little trust in the capability of the government opposite and that it will make things right.
I have to say that I do not have that belief and trust. I cannot have that belief and trust any more. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, whom I admire for his ability to twist words and to make them seem realistic, can make all the excuses he wishes to convince his colleagues that there is justification in mixing apples and oranges, or smelts and herring, to produce the desired results, but unless he produces some realistic results and acts in the best interest of the fishermen in his province, my province, or in any other province, he had better keep in close touch with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and come up with a contingency plan to avert what will become a crisis if the fishermen of Canada resort to taking action of their own because of the lack of backbone of the government.

speechtext:

All this is not Canada's doing alone. The expanding development of distant-water fisheries activities has not only preempted the opportunities of Canadian fishermen, but has resulted in excess fishing effort which has driven the stocks to their present low levels. I think this is understood by all hon. members who have spoken today. So a decrease in such distant-water fishing effort is essential to restore the stocks and the balance between resource availability and fishing capacity.
Because our fishery is naturally grown, with independent fishermen and companies fishing because they like it, but also to make money, our fleet has found it hard to compete, especially with east European fleets relatively unconcerned with economics. Our fleet is composed mainly of relatively small vessels without the capacity to move to distant fishing waters and unable to find economic markets for non-traditional species.
In an attempt to compete with foreign fleets the Canadian industry has increased the tonnage of larger Canadian vessels by 2.5 times since 1959, but has achieved only a 30 per cent increase in landings for its efforts.
Many of our fishermen are facing a desperate situation. Were things to go on as they are, communities would disappear. A basic foundation to improving matters is a rebuilding of the stocks to levels where the catch per trip of Canadian vessels can offset the unavoidable and rising costs of putting the vessels to sea. Let me say simply that we will not be able to do this on the basis of the motion presented by the hon. member for St. John's West. This would be fine if our problems could be resolved in a simple way-they cannot. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, they cannot.
We are taking a variety of steps to achieve the objective underlying this motion. We are doing so in the Law of the Sea Conference, in ICNAF, and in other negotiations. We intend to succeed and to ensure a brighter future for our fisheries and our fishermen.
For one thing we intend to make sure that our fishing industry remains, as it is now, under ownership that is overwhelmingly Canadian. We are looking toward other measures such as, in some fisheries, encouraging consolidation of marketing on the basis of restricted export licensing, to achieve greater marketing effectiveness by means of shared expertise, more promotion, and so on. Other possibilities exist to help create a stronger, more diversified industry. We are consulting the industry and fishermen, and know we have a great deal of support for certain courses of action. I hope that the members who have been so strong in supporting meaningless resolutions will be equally ready to lend their help on some of these more mundane matters, through which we may work together to build a strong and stable industry.
With all due respect to the hon. member for St. John's West and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, both of whom are members of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and who made a major contribution to that committee, I must say that the motion has left members from British Columbia, regardless of which side of
National Resources
the House they sit on, faced with the most difficult task of weighing the pros and cons of this motion and its effect on west coast fishing in particular.
I am truly surprised that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich seconded the motion without realizing the serious gap in the west coast position if the motion were accepted. His quick acceptance of the amendment by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) was a desperate grasp at reality. The motion he supported is not acceptable to the members from British Columbia on this side of the House.
This motion would impose a very severe penalty upon the west coast fishing industry. What is good for the Altantic coast is not necessarily good for the Pacific coast, and this motion will bear me out.
The boundaries of this motion would assure the Atlantic coast full protection on the continental shelf and slope to the required limit. Such an interpretation would not apply to the Pacific coast, however, as has been said earlier. What it would do is give us a protection zone extending 60 to 70 miles offshore. This is a far cry from the 200 mile limit the government is seeking.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for New Westminster is not acceptable to my colleagues from the west coast on this side of the House. Unilateral action is not an answer; indeed it is a hindrance to our international aims and commitments. What do the hon. member for St. John's West and the hon. member for New Westminster mean when they say "immediate action"? I believe they mean "unilateral action", Mr. Speaker.
The salmon enhancement program would suffer a drastic setback if this motion were passed. The proposal for hatcheries on the west coast would never come to fruition. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, and on behalf of the fishermen and the industry on the west coast, I must voice disapproval of the motion and the amendment and, when called upon, vote against both.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my maiden speech in this House I indicated to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) that I would not for a moment attempt to be a captain of his ship but I would stand on board and watch for the shallow waters, reefs, and rocks, and I would give him warning when his ship was in trouble and there was a possibility of running aground.
It is certainly no secret that we have major problems in central Canada. We are suffering from the concept of dual jurisdiction. In the arrangement by the federal government in 1930 the jurisdiction for inland fisheries was transferred from the federal government to the provinces.
The freshwater fishing industry is in a critical state-a deplorable state. Prices are depressed and costs are rising. Fishermen in central Canada are confused. On the one hand provincial jurisdiction takes care of quotas where applicable, and also licensing. The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, which is under federal jurisdiction, looks after marketing.
The corporation is several years old. It enshrines a concept of input by fishermen, but there is only one fisherman on the board. To offset that there is an advisory committee consisting of 16 fishermen. One would think their input would be sufficient and meaningful, and that they would have some say in the affairs pertaining to the corporation. I do not believe this is the case, however. A member of that advisory board told me that this is his last year on the committee, that he did not want to go back. He said it does not involve the fishermen as much as it should. They cannot advise the corporation because they do not have access to many of the reports, and their suggestions are not taken into consideration. Then the president of the corporation at the annual meeting said that the talks, meaning the resolutions that were passed at that annual meeting, will not bring about any major policy change.
I suggest that the input of fishermen to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is not significant, in the direction of the corporation. Probably the single, most blatant failure of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation lies in the area of marketing. The whole idea behind the establishment of the corporation was that it would bring about orderly marketing. There was never any talk at the time of the corporation's establishment about the processing facilities which the corporation was also going to run.
I have said before in this chamber that I come from Nova Scotia. Back in Nova Scotia we had the idea that if you wanted to set up a processing plant, the logical place to put it was by the ocean, by the harbour, by the docks where the boats come in and land their fish. That is where you should set up your processing plant.

If you go west you will find huge and beautifully modern processing plants controlled, run, and even owned by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. Of course you would expect them to be located by Lake Winnipeg or the other lakes where the catches are made. That is what you would expect; but that is not the case. There is one sitting among the grain elevators, out in the wheat fields of Transcona, and the nearest water to that processing plant is 25 miles away as the birds'fly. And that makes sense to some people! Apparently it makes sense to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) because he continually supports the idea of the plant being there.
But the biggest problem, as I said earlier, has to do with the marketing process. After all the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was set up to market fish in an orderly way. The catch, now that the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is involved, has dropped from 70 million pounds to 33 million pounds. There is a simple rule of economics which says that if demand increases and supply diminishes, price rises. But with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation we have the reverse situation. The supply has decreased by 50 per cent, but the price has risen hardly at all.
When we ask the province which deals with matters like licensing what's wrong, it says, "But that is not our problem; that is a problem for the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation." The fishermen, who are not great scholars of economics, have to sell their fish to the corporation and want to know why prices are depressed. The corporation says, "It's not really our fault; the problem is that prices are generally depressed in Canada." So, when we come to the federal minister and ask him why Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation prices are depressed in Winnipeg, he says, "It is not really a Canadian problem; the problem is that the darned price of those codfish blocks in Chicago is depressed." I confess that it is remotely conceivable that prices are depressed for that reason. But I tell you I can't make that stick when I go back to the fishermen of my area, to those Icelanders who will catch a fish if there is one to be caught, and tell them that the price of pickerel caught in Lake Winnipeg is depressed because codfish block prices in Chicago are depressed.
That is not the end of the story. I live in North Kildonan and shop at the North Kildonan Safeway. I could shop at other places, but I happen to shop at the Safeway. Every week I check the price of pickerel fillets and, you know, for the last three months pickerel fillets at the North Kildonan Safeway have been selling for $2.99 a pound. Mind you, they are alongside Captain's Choice, Highliner, and fillets of codfish, haddock and lesser species. But there was pickerel, selling for $2.99 a pound. I was excited. I said, "Oh, at long last prices have risen and there will be prosperity the like of which fishermen have never seen."
I jumped in my car and rushed off to Gimli, to participate with those celebrating these tremendously high prices. But when I got there the fishermen said, "This is strange." I learned that the corporation pays the fishermen 60 cents a pound, if they deliver to the corporation. If they do not deliver, the corporation has to take out a little money for transportation, agents, and handling fees, and fishermen could get about 42 cents per pound.
June 19, 1975

Let us suppose that fishermen have a half ton truck, on which they can load fish to take to the corporation 25 miles away. Let me point out that Gimli is not 25 miles from the lake. I was referring to the point closest to the lake. Gimli is an additional 60 miles away. So, in the heat of summer the fishermen load their fish on the half ton truck and take it to the corporation; and you can imagine the state of the fish when it reaches the corporation. The fishermen are paid, at most, 60 cents a pound. Yet there are no middlemen. The corporation does not deal with middlemen. Oh, no, it deals directly with markets.
Why do pickerel fillets sell for $2.99 a pound in the store, when the fishermen were paid only 60 cents? That is what I want to know. Why is there this difference? To me this makes no sense. Perhaps I am using the wrong schoolboy arithmetic. Perhaps there is some great formula which might make sense to a bureaucracy but, to me, it does not add up.
In closing I urge the minister to take action and to introduce a support program for fish landed and delivered to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. If the minister does not act more expeditiously on that matter than I suspect he will act on the substance of the motion now before the House, this entire debate will have been nothing but an exercise in academics.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one cannot help noticing the poor draftsmanship of the motion introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter) which, if the House were to approve this motion tonight by a majority,-and that is impossible-could place Canada in a delicate, not to say dangerous, position in the current negotiations.
What surprises me, Mr. Speaker, is that the hon. member for St. John's West or his party did not have recourse to the diplomatic style of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) before asking him to support the motion. In all probability, he was not called upon because we saw him stiffen with indignation this afternoon when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) reminded him of the adverse consequences of passing this motion, should it carry. In spite of all that, I am glad to participate in this debate, representing a population whose subsistance depends, nearly exclusively in certain places, on the fishery industry.
Hon. members who are interested in that facet of our economy are already aware that Canada and this government intend to obtain immediate improvements on the present situation of fisheries in the Atlantic through ICNAF which is now holding important sessions, and they also know that our negotiators made excellent progress at the Conference on the Law of the Sea.
The reports we received show that most countries are now gradually accepting the concept of an exclusive economic zone of 200 miles. Those are concrete facts. May I remind hon. members that the tendency gives early indications that we are rapidly moving toward the jurisdiction we seek over our resources.
Incidentally, about that Conference on the Law of the Sea, I would like to set the record straight about claims by
National Resources
the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) who suggested earlier that several delegations at the Conference on the Law of the Sea were represented on a full time basis by ministers. According to the information I have from reliable sources, people who were there on a full time basis, only Norway was represented by ministers during the whole conference. The Soviet Union sent a deputy minister who participated in the conference on a full time basis. He is a government official. A few other delegations from other countries had ministers as representatives but only on a part time basis but never has any country had, on a part time basis, four ministers at the same time, as Canada did for instance. I wanted to make those few corrections, even though I did not have the honour of attending the conference, because the information I was given is correct.
The first Conference on the Law of the Sea, held in 1958-and I think it is fit and proper to review the facts briefly-produced four international conventions, each concerning the use of renewable resources. There were first the Geneva Convention on the High Seas, the Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Continguous Zone, the Convention on Fishing and the Conservation of the Living Resources of the High Seas, and the International Convention on the Continental Shelf.
However, the 1958 conference did not result in an agreement about two vital, close related points: the extent of territorial waters as well as the nature and the limits of coastal state jurisdiction over fisheries adjacent to the coast.
A second Law of the Sea Conference held in 1960- where Canada played leading part in an effort to extend the rights of coastal states-did not succeed either in resolving those problems. In any event, Mr. Speaker, the agreements of 1958 have been the basis of a conventional law of the sea until now even though common international law or the practice generally accepted on the international scene plays an ever increasing part.
None of the four Geneva conventions has been ratified by the majority of countries. I should say that in 1958 several countries had not yet obtained their independence and that today they hesitate with reason to subscribe to a conventional law system which was established without their participation and which some of them consider imperfect.
Of those four conventions, Canada has ratified only one, the Convention on the Continental Shelf. Even if it recognizes some merit to the other conventions, the Canadian government finds them inadequate to protect the interests of Canada when it comes to safeguarding the marine environment and its renewable resources. So we have used other means to adapt the legislation to current problems: regional agreements like those that paved the way for establishing various international commissions on fishing, bilateral agreements and, if needed-and when the situation was favourable and always within the limits imposed by our adhesion to the world community-unilateral action that contributes to the development of common law.

June 19, 1975
National Resources
Following the failure of the second Law of the Sea Conference and other multilateral efforts to reach an agreement to extend the universally accepted three-mile jurisdiction, Canada adopted in 1964 the baseline system to measure the territorial sea, thus, giving Canadians exclusive fishing rights extending 12 miles from Canadian cape lines, whose sole limitation comes from traditional practices from other coastal states off the Atlantic coasts, practices which are, by the way, progressively excluded.
In 1970, Canada extended over 12 miles, on its territory, complete sovereignty over the 9-mile fishing zone and established a series of closing lines giving Canadians exclusive fishing rights in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the Bay of Fundy, Queen Charlotte Sound, Hecate Strait and Dixon Entrance as well as in its 12-mile territorial sea.
We have, Mr. Speaker, the longest closing lines in the world. One of 100 miles extends between Vancouver Island and Queen Charlotte Sound on the west coast, others close the Bay of Fundy and the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Hudson Bay to all foreign fishermen. Our fishing fleets are gradually gaining exclusive access to some of the most important fish stocks in the world.
The establishment of these closing lines affirms the jurisdiction of Canada over the conservation and the administration of fisheries over an additional territory of 80,000 square miles offshore.
Later, negotiations for phasing out traditional fishing were affected by those actions by Canada, and those negotiations fortunately brought results with all those countries, except the United States. In the latter case, a mutual agreement of fisheries, renegotiated for two years, provides that Canadian and American fishermen will continue to fish up to three miles from the shores of either country.
It is no doubt important, Mr. Speaker, to point out to the House and to Canadian fishermen some of the results due to the establishment by Canada of fisheries closing lines for foreign countries and the efforts we made to suspend gradually the rights of some countries. For example, Britain as well as Norway have left the St. Lawrence. Denmark is still fishing in certain restricted bases which it will leave in less than a year. Portugal will also leave the area in less than a year and Spain in a year. Canada has done all that, Mr. Speaker, by resorting to a policy recognized as firm but reasonable according to traditions in international affairs.
Canada has also taken special steps in 1970 to protect the delicate marine environment of the Arctic. To that effect, it has set up a 100-mile pollution control area. Soon afterwards, a similar antipollution legislation was passed for the exclusive fisheries areas in the St. Lawrence River, Bay of Fundy, Dixon Entrance, Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound.
As all members know, we have not yet achieved total success within ICNAF. Canadian fishermen on the Atlantic coast have witnessed their fish catches diminish by 40 per cent in recent years. I could pursue my speech, Mr. Speaker, but I can see you are growing impatient. Still I should like to say that the most important factor at the present time, Mr. Speaker, and thus I shall conclude, is

that almost all nations believe that an exclusive economic zone will soon be established.
Canadians especially are all in favour of such a policy. The facts show that even before the present crisis the government and fisheries and marine services officials had taken the initiative with a view to exercising greater control over our coastal waters.
Meanwhile, Mr. Speaker, the motion proposed by the hon. member for St. John's West would not add anything.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of the Treasury Board) moved:
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN MAIN ESTIMATES FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31,1976
speechtext: That the main estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1976, except those items disposed of at earlier sittings, and less the amounts voted in interim supply, be concurred in.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN MAIN ESTIMATES FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31,1976
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN MAIN ESTIMATES FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31,1976
speechtext: Agreed.

Motion agreed to.
Mr. Chretien thereupon moved that Bill C-64, for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending March 31, 1976, be read the first time and be printed.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.
Mr. Chretien there upon moved that Bill C-64, for granting Her Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1976, be read the second time and referred to the Committee of the Whole.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Laniel in the Chair.

Clauses 2 to 4 inclusive agreed to.
On Clause 5-Appropriation charged.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN MAIN ESTIMATES FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31,1976
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the President of the Treasury Board for clarification of this clause. I know this is not debate and I do not intend to debate, but because of a previous incident on a prior appropriation act I should like to ask the minister if he could give us a firm assurance that clause 5 may be a standard clause or, if not, to give us the precise purpose of clause 5. On the previous occasion we did not get the appropriate explanation, and a precedent was set in this House which should not have been set.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN MAIN ESTIMATES FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31,1976
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the form of this bill is the same as that of similar bills passed in previous years and does not contain authorization for additional loans; as far as I know, the same formula is used here as in the other circumstances: this I guarantee the House.

Clause 5 agreed to.
Clause 6 agreed to.

Schedule agreed to.
Clause 1 agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN MAIN ESTIMATES FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31,1976
speechtext: When shall the bill be read the third time? By leave now?

speechtext: By leave now.

Agreed.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.
